items.title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
items.summary: Poundland's bosses are filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators to the business.
items.body:
Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
- Published
Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.
The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.
"This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC.
The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).
Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case.
"We stand ready to support the workforce however we can."
The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.
The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.
It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal Â£1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.
Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse.
It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off.
Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.
It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.
It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.
- The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisis 
  - Published21 November 2025
- Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer 
  - Published13 October
A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allow creditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff. The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.
If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.
These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested in taking on between 200 and 250 stores.
Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.
More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.
Bally Auluk, a national officer at the Usdaw shopworkers union, said this week had been "incredibly distressing" for Poundland staff.
He claimed staff were having to "watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract Â£30m from a business it bought for Â£1".
He said Williams had "reluctantly" kicked off the administration process, to give the business time to find a rescue deal, adding that Usdaw was urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider.
The uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future has left some staff fearful about the future of their jobs.
Staff at Poundland's customer support centre in Walsall, some dressed as the Poundland "Pound Hound" mascot, held a protest on Thursday.
One employee said they were trying to "save our jobs".
Situation 'wholly avoidable'
There is also a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable".
"As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week.
He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds which help it run its day-to-day business.
"I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added.
In the memo, seen by the BBC, Williams said the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made".
Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.
Gordon Brothers has lined up AlixPartners as administrators.
Get in touch
Do you work for Poundland? Share your experience.

items.title: Andy Burnham pushes for answers as Poundland edges towards collapse - what next for retailer?
items.summary: Andy Burnham has now said he is willing to demand answers over the retailer's owners' handling of a sales process. The Prime Minister said it was a 'deeply worrying time' for staff and their families.
items.body:
Andy Burnham pushes for answers as Poundland edges towards collapse - what next for retailer?
Poundland could disappear from the High Street within days as Andy Burnham asks questions over how its owners handled a sales process.
Thousands of nervous staff are waiting to hear what will happen to the discount retailer after it filed a notice to appoint administrators with the High Court today.
This will give the business, bought by US investment firm Gordon Brothers for less than £1 last year, some breathing room – ten days – to find a rescue deal. AlixPartners is poised to take over a potential insolvency process.
But the Poundland brand and its 600 shops will not be sold as a whole, leading to a carve-up of the 36-year old retailer, meaning jobs are at risk at any shops that are not bought.
And on Thursday night, the Prime Minister said he is ready to demand answers from owners amid a 'deeply worrying time' for staff and their families.
Burnham told The Telegraph: 'We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case.'
Battle for survival: The fate of Poundland's near 12,000 staff hangs in the balance.
It would mark the biggest high street collapse since Debenhams closed its doors in 2021 with the loss of 12,000 jobs.
Job losses could hit 600 shops and a distribution centre in Makerfield, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s constituency, which employs around 270 people.
Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds also said he was ‘very much concerned’ and would push for answers as workers and bosses seethe over its failure to find a buyer.
He told The Telegraph: ‘If it is true that it was not necessary to put the business into administration then the present owners will have to account for that.’
Why has Poundland struggled?
Chains like Poundland are battling shoppers with constrained budgets while costs, such as employing people, have increased – following Government moves to hike wages and employer National Insurance contributions. Savvier shoppers are looking for cheaper online alternatives, including Amazon, Temu and TikTok Shop.
Former owners, the Warsaw-listed Pepco Group, made some wrong moves that did not go down well with its customers, including putting Pepco clothing in its shops.
Its most recent woes stem back to last year, when it narrowly avoided collapsing into administration. The chain was sold in June 2025 to US firm Gordon Brothers for a nominal €1 amid 'challenging trading conditions'.
By November 2025, around 100 Poundland shops had been shut or earmarked for closure. Two months later, as part of its radical turnaround plan, Poundland had shut 149 stores with 2,200 job losses.
But this year, Poundland bosses insisted it was turning a corner, pointing to like-for-like sales growth of 3.3 per cent in the three months to September 26.
Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month: 'Our recovery plan is working, thanks to our investment in simple low pricing and new ranges, powered by our new in-house teams.'
Why is there a dispute between Poundland’s owners and its bosses?
Both shop workers’ union Usdaw and Poundland’s management have accused Gordon Brothers of mishandling a sales process, which it kicked off at the beginning of September.
The union met with the minister for the future of work, Kate Dearden, on Wednesday, amid warnings of what would be the biggest High Street collapse in years.
Three directors, appointed less than a fortnight ago, this week walked out following a dramatic dispute with owners Gordon Brothers.
Hours later the retailer’s management hit out at the owners, calling the process ‘unexpected, unwanted and avoidable’.
Government adviser David Bickerton is set to ask ‘fairly basic questions of senior people around Poundland’ in order to ‘establish what the situation is,’ on behalf of the business secretary, the Financial Times reported.
What does a notice to appoint administrators mean?
‘Filing a notice of intention isn’t administration itself,’ explains Julie Palmer, managing partner at real estate advisory group BTG.
Instead, it effectively keeps the wolves from the door for up to ten business days of protection and helps the firm preserve cash.
She added: ‘If an appointment follows, the administrators take control of the company from the directors. Their first duty is to try to rescue it as a going concern.
'If that isn’t possible, they aim for a better result for creditors than liquidation would give. In practice that usually means a sale, either of the whole business or in parts. For staff and customers, stores normally keep trading while that happens, but the risk is that the business is broken up, with stronger stores sold and weaker ones closed.’
Who could buy the shops?
Owner Gordon Brothers rejected a takeover offer from Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group – despite management and unions arguing this was the best deal on the table.
This would have been for the whole business, including its brand and full store estate.
But now it seems like other major retailers, especially those with grand expansion plans, could pick up some shops from Poundland.
The owner of The Range, Homebase and Wilko – known as Britain’s ‘Del Boy Billionaire’ – is thought to be interested. Chris Dawson, 74, who runs CDS Superstores, acquired the Wilko brand out of administration in 2023.
Dawson got his nickname, the 'Del Boy billionaire', via the press as a reference to his yellow Lamborghini Urus, which has a personalised number plate 'DE11 BOY', a homage to the character Del Boy Trotter from the classic TV show Only Fools and Horses.
Dawson started his career as a market trader, before founding The Range and scaling it to a major high street chain. He has since acquired Wilko and Homebase out of administration.
Chris Dawson, 74, runs CDS Superstores, which owns The Range, Homebase and Wilko
Poundstretcher owner Fortress is also understood to be looking at buying shops. The rival discount retailer runs more than 300 shops in the UK.
Supermarket Lidl also hopes to be able to snap up some of its stores if the retailer fails to sell the whole company. The discounter is pushing ahead with a major expansion mission.
TG Jones owner is also understood to be interested in buying parts of the Poundland business.
The private equity group owns Britain's WH Smith shops, now known as TG Jones stores and previously bought ailing accessories chain Claire's, Hobbycraft and The Original Factory Shop.
All Claire's standalone shops in the UK and Ireland stopped trading earlier this year after its financial woes saw it fall into administration twice in a year.
Are shops open and will staff be paid?
Poundland shops are currently open and operating business as usual.
But Poundland's managing director Barry Williams wrote a letter to around 12,000, accusing the retailer’s owner of limiting the chain's access to funding.
This has effectively prevented bosses from making routine payments, with suppliers now worried they will not be paid on time this week, according to Sky News.
But sources close to the crisis talks insisted that this should not prevent staff from being paid at the end of the month.
Williams told staff: 'I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement.'
Gordon Brothers are accused of breaching the terms of an asset-based lending facility by failing to submit a budget to the shareholders on time despite an agreed grace period – with the business now outperforming those forecasts, Sky News reported.
Julie Palmer, managing partner at real estate advisory group BTG, says that in this situation, ‘existing commitments such as payroll and supplier invoices can still be met from cash already available‘.
But bosses cannot ‘draw further funds to cover anything beyond that,’ she says, which poses a problem as retailers typically draw from these loans in the autumn to buy Christmas stock - before repaying from festive sales in December and January.
She added: ‘If a lender has concerns about longer-term viability, it may simply be unwilling to increase its exposure by funding that stock build, particularly when it can’t be sure who will own the business, or what shape it will be in, by the time the money needs to come back.
‘That leaves management with very little room to manoeuvre. It limits their ability to buy stock or take on new commitments, and puts directors in a difficult position, because they must be confident the company can meet its liabilities before taking on new ones. Once credit insurers pull back and suppliers start asking for payment up front, the squeeze tightens quickly.’

items.body:
Landsec, owner of one of the UK’s leading retail and hospitality portfolios, has welcomed Indetix-owned Bershka to Westgate Oxford as leading brands continue to invest in the destination.
The new store opened today (29 October, 2026), bringing one of Europe’s most recognisable youth fashion brands to Westgate Oxford. Popular with Gen Z, Bershka strengthens the destination’s appeal to a generation that is increasingly influencing how brands think about physical retail.
The signing further strengthens Landsec’s long-standing relationship with Inditex and reflects continued confidence from one of the world’s largest fashion groups, in Landsec’s retail destinations.
Bershka’s arrival also reflects continued demand from major international brands looking to grow within high-performing retail destinations. With more than 17 million visitors each year and a mix of local residents, students and tourists, Westgate Oxford continues to attract brands looking to connect with a broad customer base in the heart of one of the UK’s most visited cities.
The opening follows a series of recent new additions at Westgate Oxford, including Sephora and LEGO, whose new store attracted significant crowds on opening day. Together with Bershka’s arrival, these signings highlight the continued appeal of Westgate Oxford to leading international brands.
Pablo Sueiras, head of retail & hospitality leasing at Landsec, said: “Bershka is a fantastic addition to Westgate Oxford and further reinforces the destination’s position as a leading retail and leisure destination. As retailers focus investment on locations that can deliver reach, engagement and growth, Westgate Oxford continues to attract sought-after brands and concepts. With a loyal Gen Z customer base, Bershka brings a fresh dimension to our fashion offer and enhances the appeal of the destination for both new and existing visitors.”

items.body:
Frasers Plus Braehead has secured another major market first, with Bath & Body Works set to open its first standalone store in Scotland at the retail and leisure destination this winter.
Opening ahead of Christmas, the new store, spanning more than 2,000 sq ft, will add a significant new gifting offer to the destination at the busiest time in the retail calendar. Bath & Body Works’ established appeal across fragrance, beauty and seasonal gifting will give shoppers another compelling reason to visit Frasers Plus Braehead.
The signing enhances Frasers Plus Braehead’s beauty and lifestyle line-up, joining Rituals, Boots, LUSH, M&S and TK Maxx, alongside Scotland’s largest Superdrug store. With White Stuff also due to open shortly, the destination continues to build a varied brand mix for shoppers across the region.
The signing follows the recent opening of SuperPark’s first UK location at Braehead, further reinforcing the destination’s appeal to leading national and international brands.
Rachel Scott, head of leasing at Global Mutual, commented: “Bath & Body Works’ decision to select Frasers Plus Braehead for its first standalone Scottish store is a significant endorsement of the destination’s regional reach and the momentum behind our evolving offer.
“Bath & Body Works will broaden our beauty offer across body care, home fragrance and gifting, while giving shoppers access to the full standalone store experience. Opening ahead of Christmas, it will introduce a strong new gifting proposition that complements the wider destination at a key trading moment.”
A spokesperson from Bath & Body Works, said: “Opening our first standalone Scottish store is an important milestone for Bath & Body Works, and Frasers Plus Braehead is the ideal location for this next step in our growth.
“The destination’s strong regional draw and impressive mix of leading retail brands made it a natural choice for our debut. We look forward to bringing the full Bath & Body Works experience to Braehead and building meaningful relationships with customers across Scotland.”
Bath & Body Works is due to open at Frasers Plus Braehead in winter 2026. For more information about Frasers Plus Braehead visit their website here: https://frasersplusbraehead.co.uk/

items.body:
FatFace has today announced the opening of a new store in Altrincham this autumn, bringing the lifestyle brand to the town for the first time.
Measuring 1,550sq ft, the new store will allow customers to explore and purchase iconic items from FatFace’s core range and the newest winter collection, featuring seasonal knitwear, nightwear, occasionwear and gifting. The collection also includes FatFace’s latest collaboration with the V&A, inspired by the whimsical world of Wonderland.
The Altrincham store will create six jobs upon opening, with further hiring underway. New team members will enjoy generous staff discounts, access to wellbeing services, learning and development resources, and flexible working opportunities.
Karen Johnston, stores director at FatFace, commented: “We are excited to be opening our new store in Greater Manchester. Altrincham has a thriving retail environment with mix of independent and established brands, making it a great fit for FatFace. We’re looking forward to becoming part of the local community and welcoming customers through our doors.”
A leading British lifestyle brand, FatFace currently operates 172 stores in the UK and seven stores in ROI. The brand also continues to grow its international digital presence across Europe through NEXT Label and Zalando.
As a B Corp Certified company, FatFace focuses on its key pillars of product, planet and community.

items.body:
PATRÓN EL ALTO, the exceptionally aged tequila, is passionately crafted from the highest-quality 100% Blue Weber Agave that is cultivated in the highest parts of Jalisco, Mexico, where the sweetest agave grows. Best enjoyed neat or on the rocks, the unique blend of PATRÓN Extra Añejo, Añejo and Reposado results in a unique high-end tequila that beckons to be savored.
- Savor the soft, sweet aromatic notes of agave, dried fruit and toasted wood when you pour a glass of PATRÓN EL ALTO. The light gold, captivatingly bright colour is a hint of what is to come. Delightfully bright flavours emerge, tasting of apricots, vanilla, almonds and cooked agave. PATRÓN EL ALTO is impressively smooth, subtly sweet and best enjoyed neat or on the rocks.
- We grow the highest-quality 100% Blue Weber Agave in the highest parts of the Atotonilco El Alto region in Jalisco, Mexico, that yields the sweetest agaves and which inspired the name for PATRÓN EL ALTO. After we harvest the sweet agave, we ground it with ancient volcanic stone, bake it for days in clay ovens and masterfully age it.
- PATRÓN EL ALTO is composed of PATRÓN Extra Añejo—aged for four years—blended with exceptional PATRÓN Añejo and Reposado tequilas, resulting in a uniquely innovative, beautifully crafted expression of bold and sweet flavors.
- PATRÓN tequila is widely available in the UK, with El Alto bottles available to purchase from retailers including Selfridges and the brand’s Amazon.com storefront. Link here.
- Reposado means “rested” in Spanish, and it signifies the period when the tequila ages in oak barrels to develop its exquisitely smooth character. PATRÓN Reposado is aged at least four months in oak barrels at Hacienda PATRÓN in Mexico, developing a complex yet balanced ultra-premium flavour profile that works beautifully in cocktails and long drinks, from a refreshing PATRÓN Paloma to a Spicy Margarita.
- As the tequila ages, it absorbs the rich characteristics of the wood from the barrels, which imparts unique depth and smoothness to this world-famous tequila.
- Only the highest-quality ingredients are used to craft this spirit, which maintains the roasted agave flavours unique to PATRÓN mingled in perfect harmony with hints of light oak and vanilla.
- Perfect to sip neat or in a cocktail, the aging process turns the liquid to a marvellous shade of light amber gold, imbuing it with a light oaky flavour alongside big, cooked agave notes.
- PATRÓN tequila is widely available in the UK, with 70cl PATRÓN Reposado bottles found at major supermarkets and Amazon.com.
- The world’s first super-premium silver tequila, handcrafted from the finest 100% Blue Weber Agave, PATRÓN Silver is perfect for sipping or mixing in a wide range of cocktails, including the classic PATRÓN Margarita.
- PATRÓN Silver captures the unaged spirit of agave, revealing its sweet and smooth flavour while offering a crisp, clean taste. Made using a handcrafted distillation process unique to PATRÓN, this clear spirit is produced with only three natural, high quality ingredients—100% Blue Weber Agave, yeast and water.
- Made with the finest 100% Blue Weber Agave and handcrafted using time-honoured traditional methods, PATRÓN Silver is a testament to authentic Mexican heritage and to the spirit of the agave plant.
- PATRÓN tequila is widely available in the UK, with 70cl PATRÓN Silver bottles found at major supermarkets and Amazon.com.
- PATRÓN Miniatures bring the brand’s premium tequila range into a convenient 5cl format, available across PATRÓN Silver, Reposado and El Alto.
- PATRÓN Silver is a clear, crisp and smooth tequila made from 100% Blue Weber Agave, with a clean profile that makes it ideal for sipping or mixing into cocktails.
- PATRÓN Reposado is aged for at least four months in oak barrels, developing a smooth, rounded character with notes of roasted agave, light oak and vanilla.
- PATRÓN El Alto is an exceptionally aged expression combining PATRÓN Extra Añejo, Añejo and Reposado tequilas, creating a rich and complex profile with notes of agave, dried fruit, toasted wood, apricot, vanilla and almond.
- Each miniature offers the same distinctive character and craftsmanship of its full-size expression in a smaller format.

items.body:
Very, the online retailer operated by The Very Group, has unveiled a price commitment which guarantees the price customers pay on Black Friday offers will always be the cheapest, even if the same item is reduced further during its Black Friday event.
The Price Promise covers eligible Black Friday discounted products across all categories, from fashion, electrical and toys to home, beauty and sports.
Eligible Black Friday purchases will be protected against subsequent Very price reductions throughout the entire Black Friday event, from 28 October to 4 December.
Robbie Feather, chief executive officer, The Very Group, said: “Our Price Promise is all about giving customers greater confidence that they’re getting the best deal. For Black Friday, we’re going even further.
“One of the biggest decisions customers face during Black Friday is deciding whether to buy now or wait to see if prices fall even further.
“Our Price Promise removes that uncertainty. Customers can shop our deals as soon as they see them, safe in the knowledge that if we reduce the price of an eligible product later in the event, they won’t miss out.”
Very’s Black Friday commitment covers eligible Black Friday discounted lines across all categories, and protects the price customers pay against subsequent price reductions by Very for the duration of the Black Friday event.
If an eligible product bought during the Black Friday event is later reduced by Very before 4 December 2026, customers can contact Very Customer Services by that date and, subject to the terms of the promise, claim back the difference.
Alongside the Black Friday price promise, Very is also offering customers an everyday price promise across thousands of products within its electrical and toys categories.

items.body:
Leading sports nutrition brand Warrior® has launched a new line of accessible protein, tapping into growing mainstream demand for affordable, everyday protein.
Now officially available in Asda stores nationwide, Warrior Serious Protein offers consumers a convenient way to incorporate more protein into their daily routines, for just £12.50 per 500g tub.
Available in three classic flavours – Chocolate, Strawberry and Vanilla Milkshake – Serious Protein delivers 24g of protein, 110 calories and just 0.3g of fat per 30g. Designed for everyday use, it can be enjoyed in post-workout shakes, with breakfast or as an afternoon protein top-up.
Each tub contains 16 servings, and the new innovative formula combines soy protein isolate, skimmed milk powder, casein and glutamine peptides, with no added sugar. It is also suitable for vegetarians.
The launch comes amidst rising whey protein prices alongside growing consumer demand for protein products. Increasing interest in fitness and wellness, combined with greater awareness of the importance of maintaining muscle mass among GLP-1 users, are fuelling this growth.
Kieran Fisher, founder and CEO of Warrior®, said “We wanted to create a protein powder that delivers on the fundamentals consumers are looking for, which is high protein content, great-tasting flavours and an accessible price point.
“There’s no avoiding the fact that the cost of whey has increased globally due to high demand, so we’ve looked at how we can offer consumers an accessible alternative without compromising on the things that matter.
“Serious Protein is designed to give more people an affordable way to hit their protein goals. It also sits alongside our bestselling range of whey protein tubs and bars, giving consumers and our retail partners even more choice as demand for protein shows no sign of slowing down.”
Serious Protein is made in Warrior’s own BRCGS certified factory in Trafford Park, Manchester, where the brand has been producing sports nutrition since 2008.
Warrior Serious Protein is available now in Asda stores nationwide, Amazon and at www.teamwarrior.com.

items.title: Union in plea to save Poundland from administration, with 12,000 jobs at risk
items.summary: Owner Gordon Brothers files notice of intent to begin process after rejecting management-backed rescue bid Business live – latest updates The shop workers’ union Usdaw has urged Poundland’s owners to reconsider a decision to prepare the budget chain for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk. Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. Continue reading...
items.body:
The shop workers’ union Usdaw has urged Poundland’s owners to reconsider a decision to prepare the budget chain for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk.
Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.
The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought.
Gordon Brothers previously rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland. It bought the struggling chain for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.
Only one bidder, Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-owned company, was interested in buying the entire chain and working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, the chief executive.
Gordon Brothers is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer, which was worth less than the £30m in debts that Gordon Brothers took on when it bought the chain.
The threat of administration leaves thousands of shop workers facing uncertainty in the run-up to Christmas. Rival cut-price retailers, including Poundstretcher, The Range and B&M, have reportedly expressed an interest in taking on some Poundland stores.
Bally Auluk, national officer of the Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers, said: “It has been an incredibly distressing week for Poundland staff who have had to watch from the sidelines as a multibillion-pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1.
“We are urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider and to prioritise a unified buyer who will protect the livelihoods of [more than] 11,000 people.”
Williams wrote to workers this week saying the rejection of the bid from Martin Property Group was “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”.
The board of Poundland said on Thursday: “We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment.”
The board said the notice of the intention to appoint administrators had been filed “in order to bring stability” as “despite enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole”. Poundland would be “working closely with our advisors to identify and deliver the best possible outcome”.
Gordon Brothers hired the advisory company Alvarez & Marsal in August to oversee a sale of the business at a reported price of £30m, fuelling fears of a breakup, despite improved trading.
Poundland, founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, was the first UK-wide chain based on a single price. However, it now offers a broader range of price points and goods in a similar way to its rival Poundstretcher, which was founded in 1981.
Rising costs and heavy competition from chains such as Savers, Home Bargains and B&M, as well as from the major supermarkets, have meant pound shop chains have been gradually disappearing.
Poundworld closed its 350 stores in 2018, and Poundland bought its rival 99p Stores in 2015. Poundland then closed about 200 of its then 800 UK stores in a restructuring last year.
In 2020, Poundstretcher was due to close about half its then 270 stores in a rescue restructure but it now has more than 300 outlets after being bought by Majestic Wine’s owner, Fortress, in 2024.
The board of Poundland said the latest sale process for Poundland had attracted offers from several established retailers “which collectively cover a significant part of the business” and that “offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs”.
Five initially interested parties include the US company Fortress, which is thought to want to take fewer than half of Poundland’s stores to add to its existing chain.
CDS, owner of The Range, and B&M are understood to be considering a bid for at least some stores.

items.title: England captain Itoje lands Snoop Dogg-linked sponsorship deal
items.summary: England captain Maro Itoje has signed a deal with Swansea City sponsor AG1 ahead of next month’s Nations Championship at Twickenham. The Saracens forward has penned a two-year agreement to become an athlete ambassador for the wellness brand, which makes drinks supplements. The lock joins actor Hugh Jackman, racing driver Sir Lewis Hamilton and sprinter [...]
items.body:
England captain Itoje lands Snoop Dogg-linked sponsorship deal
England captain Maro Itoje has signed a deal with Swansea City sponsor AG1 ahead of next month’s Nations Championship at Twickenham.
The Saracens forward has penned a two-year agreement to become an athlete ambassador for the wellness brand, which makes drinks supplements.
The lock joins actor Hugh Jackman, racing driver Sir Lewis Hamilton and sprinter Allyson Felix within the AG1 roster as England prepare for a month of international rugby in which they will face New Zealand, Japan and Australia before a finals weekend at Allianz Stadium in London.
AG1 this summer became the front-of-shirt sponsor of Championship high-flyers Swansea City, whose eclectic ownership consortium includes minority holdings for rapper Snoop Dogg, lifestyle guru Martha Stewart and footballer Luka Modric.
The wellness brand offers a green health powder, mixed with water, as its primary product, with the Swansea deal AG1’s first venture in football.
The Chris Ashenden-founded brand, which in 2022 raised $115m in a funding round that valued AG1 at $1.2bn, also has agreements with the wider England Rugby organisation.
Itoje on board
Tim Harrington of AG1 said: “Maro embodies exactly what we look for in a partner – someone who lives our product, not just endorses it. His story, on and off the pitch, is proof that consistency compounds. We’re proud to help him tell it.”
Their sponsorship of Swansea City bucked a trend of shirts being fronted by gambling organisations following a voluntary ban of the sector in the same advertising space across the Premier League.
“The partnership will roll out across further film,” a statement read, “including the brand’s ‘Morning Person’ format ft. Maro – as well as longform press, podcast content and a UK event programme in the months ahead, with further details to follow.”
England’s autumn campaign will likely see Itoje extend his number of caps beyond the 102 he currently has.

items.title: What Nike’s Jordan pullback means for Foot Locker
items.summary: With Jordan accounting for roughly 25% of Foot Locker’s revenue, the athletics retailer will have some gaps to fill next year.
items.body:
Nike’s earnings earlier this month signaled a longer turnaround timeline for the activewear giant, but one of the retailer’s biggest problem areas could deal damage to its wholesale partners’ prospects as well.
The Jordan brand is a crucial piece of the puzzle for Foot Locker’s turnaround. But the most recent quarter made clear that Jordan will require more time to get healthy.
While Jordan brought in $8.7 billion in fiscal 2024 for Nike, the iconic brand is down about 20% from that benchmark. In Nike’s latest quarter, Jordan revenue fell in the mid-teens, and CEO Elliott Hill said the company would be pulling back on retro Jordan launches to correct for an oversupply.
“We’ve discussed it with our wholesale partners,” Hill said earlier this month. “Together, we will restore balance to the marketplace to create a foundation for more profitable and sustainable growth.”
In the meantime, though, that means more pain for Foot Locker, which saw comps fall 3.6% in Q2. Parent company Dick’s Sporting Goods, which bought Foot Locker for $2.4 billion last year, already drastically lowered Foot Locker’s full-year outlook in August. The retailer now expects Foot Locker comps to be flat or fall as much as 2%, compared to previous expectations of up to 3% growth.
A pullback on Jordan retro products complicates that picture further, analysts say, pinning Foot Locker’s exposure to Jordan at roughly 25% of revenues.
“If Jordan is down 30% next year, [Dick’s] has a hole to fill at Foot Locker, which we don't think can be replaced by other brands due to the [average selling price] differential,” BNP Paribas Equity Research senior analyst Laurent Vasilescu wrote Monday.
Specifically, Vasilescu estimates Foot Locker will take a roughly $550 million sales hit starting in the spring of 2027 unless it finds replacements for the Jordan volume.
Foot Locker is the largest wholesale partner for Jordan, with the basketball brand doing an approximate $1.85 billion for the retailer, Vasilescu estimates. While Foot Locker could flex up with partners like Vans and New Balance, the lower prices of those products will require Foot Locker to sell a higher volume.
BMO Capital Markets’ analyst Kelly Crago similarly flagged concerns about Foot Locker’s upcoming financials, including a cautious view of Foot Locker’s “ability to comp positively in FY27.” Crago estimates the Jordan pullback will have a 250- to 550-basis-point impact on Foot Locker’s comps that year.
“Given expected [Foot Locker] weakness, we believe [Dick’s] may need to rethink FL's cost structure,” Crago wrote Monday.
That could include shuttering Foot Locker’s European business, which accounts for about 20% of Foot Locker’s sales but is a roughly $115 million drag on profitability. Or, Crago suggested, the company could sell WSS or close down Champs.
“Whatever [Dick’s] chooses to do, we see a smaller [Foot Locker] as a further incremental risk to [Nike],” Crago said.

items.title: Value on show | In focus: Price-marked packs
items.summary: Price-marked packs (PMPs) have long been a key indicator of value for money in convenience stores. But the cost-of-living crisis has brought them more sharply into focus. As always, detail matters. Which products should retailers offer in PMPs? What are the profit margins? Is there… This story continues at Value on show | In focus: Price-marked packs Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
As always, detail matters. Which products should retailers offer in PMPs? What are the profit margins? Is there a danger that independent stores could have too many PMPs? If so, how many is too many?
Tight budgets
John O’Neill, retail operations controller at wholesaler and symbol group operator Parfetts, strongly believes in the benefits of PMPs, particularly when customers’ budgets are stretched. He says: “At a time when consumers watch every penny, clear pricing removes hesitation and speeds up decision-making.
PMPs build trust and help maintain sales volume on everyday items where shoppers benchmark against supermarkets. Demand for value will remain strong, which makes PMPs essential for competitiveness and preserving customer loyalty across core categories.”
Parfetts offers PMPs on more than 250 lines in its own Go Local range and says it tries hard to preserve profit margins, but O’Neill adds that “over-reliance on PMPs can restrict pricing flexibility and erode overall margins, especially on slower-moving lines”.
He advises that getting the mix right between PMPs, bestsellers and standard packs is key, giving retailers the room to protect profits while still “reassuring budget-conscious shoppers on value”.
Staying flexible
O’Neill adds: “Combining targeted PMPs with strong promotional activity and personal service allows independent retailers to highlight exceptional value while retaining the flexibility needed to protect overall basket profitability.”
Almost everybody agrees on the potential benefits of PMPs. Shaun Whelan, head of convenience at Link Snacks, the maker of Peperami, says: “Price-marked packs remain a vital mechanic across wholesale and convenience, helping wholesalers support their retail customers with clear value messaging and strong rate-of-sale. Independent retailers continue to look to wholesalers for products that deliver shopper confidence while also driving cash margin and repeat purchase.”
Securing prices
Within any particular product range, it makes sense to identify the key sellers for PMPs. In Peperami’s case, Whelan advises that this means the £1.25 PMP single sticks, available in Original and Firestick flavours, alongside five-packs, the best-selling SKU within the meat snacks category.
Psychologically, PMPs can also have the effect of making customers feel that retailers are making a genuine effort to help them in a time of economic difficulty.
Marta Valles Sanchez, marketing director at Takis Europe, says: “During the current cost-of-living crisis, retailers who stock PMPs can appear to be on the shopper’s side by doing the responsible thing and securing prices, which encourages customer loyalty.”
It is always worth remembering that the role played by PMPs in stores changes over time. Lauren George, external communications director at Mars Wrigley, says: “A PMP is no longer a short-term mechanic available for a set period and then disappearing.
Shoppers expect to see them, and 80% of retailers say PMPs give shoppers confidence in the price, up five percentage points on last year. This has influenced what retailers put on their shelves.
“Asked why they bought the products they did, 29% of convenience retailers pointed to the price-mark itself, up from 16% a year ago. Only customer demand and a wholesale promotion came up more often.”
Crucial moment
George adds that Mars Wrigley expects this trend to continue. Confectionery is generally bought on impulse, usually in the few seconds standing at the fixture, and a PMP minimises hesitation. Independents benefit more than anybody, says George, with 37% specifically looking to buy price-marked confectionery against 35% across total convenience.
Mars Wrigley is among many manufacturers who supply a wide range of PMPs but also advise against having too many in-store. George says: “A PMP works because it stands out from what is around it. Put one on everything, and it stops registering with consumers. The retailer has also given away the ability to price for the occasions where the shopper is not thinking about price at all.”
Considered mix
Jake Carty, category controller at Pladis, owner of McVitie’s, agrees. He says: “Ultimately, a considered mix is key. Step one is for retailers to identify the missions in-store, then step two is to use PMPs strategically, rather than treating them as a one-size-fits-all solution.”
Carty adds that finding the right balance can mean spreading your PMP range across both best-selling and high-rotation lines, together with new, standard and premium options.
Manufacturers are often helpful when it comes to deciding where and how to market PMPs in-store. Ross Davison, head of convenience at Kepak’s food division, which produces Rustlers, says it isn’t just the basics that see a sales boost with PMPs. He says: “Well-merchandised price-marked packs will even prompt consumers to purchase products that weren’t originally on their shopping list.”
Ed Merrett, wholesaler controller at PepsiCo, adds that PMPs can also be a useful tool to give new products a boost. He says: “They’re a proven way to tempt shoppers into trying new launches. In fact, 63% of new product packs sold are PMPs, which has risen from 59% over the last year.
“But retailers shouldn’t forget that sharing bags dominate this space, accounting for 73% of PMP new product sales. This means stocking new launches from best-selling brands like Walkers and Doritos in PMP format can help to simultaneously boost shopper trust and basket spend.”
As well as on new products, retailers can make sure they use PMPs to support more general trends such as the increasing pressure for unhealthy foods to be penalised and healthy equivalents to get a boost. Stuart Graham, head of convenience and impulse at KP Snacks, draws particular attention to the firm’s range of nuts.
He says: “Exempt from HFSS restrictions and backed by strong consumer demand, KP Nuts deliver on both natural health credentials, including high protein, and great taste. Suitable for a variety of needs, KP Nuts PMPs are perfect for consumers looking for a natural protein boost post-workout, or an evening savoury treat that’s great for sharing with friends and family.”
Building trust
Manufacturers can also help with specific promotions based on PMPs that can have an immediate effect on sales, such as Yazoo’s work with several UK convenience stores (see panel). Soft drinks maker AG Barr is another supplier that has increased its PMP range to boost sales. Head of category Sharon Warburton says: “We continue to see PMPs reinforcing value to shoppers and in many cases driving retail sales through offering transparency and trust.”
He adds: “The soft drinks category is one area that is particularly delivering on this. As the number one PMP category, with 40% of all soft drinks listings in independent retail being a PMP, they provide a powerful dual benefit: not only do they address shopper demand for value, but they are often not subject to the shrinkflation challenges seen in other categories.”
Harnessing the expertise of manufacturers
Bob Mulder, managing director, Friesland Campina
Several convenience stores took part in a collaborative trial with flavoured milk brand Yazoo to boost sales. The stores included Broadway Convenience in Edinburgh, St John’s Budgens in Kenilworth, Warwickshire, and Tenby Stores in Pembrokeshire.
The trial focused on increasing PMP availability alongside improving chilled displays and using dedicated point-of-sale material. It resulted in an average increase in sales of Yazoo PMPs of 89%, with Broadway Convenience managing an impressive 235% sales uplift.
Bob Mulder, managing director at Yazoo’s owner, Friesland Campina, says the company believes that, despite the cost-of-living crisis, shoppers still enjoy buying treats that are budget-friendly. He says: “In this economic climate, PMPs play a critical role in reassuring consumers who are savvier than ever about their spending. While shoppers refuse to compromise on taste or quality, they actively seek clear pricing and strong value perceptions upfront.
“PMPs directly fulfil this need by building consumer confidence and trust at the fixture, particularly within the impulse-driven convenience channel, where spontaneous pick-me-up purchases are common.”
PMPs on the rise
Lauren George, external communications manager, Mars Wrigley
Tom Fender, director, TWC
Sales of PMPs have been increasing this year, according to figures from market analyst Worldpanel, but this needs to be seen in the context of broader rises in convenience store trading.
Using the Worldpanel figures, Mars Wrigley’s external communications manager, Lauren George, says: “Convenience stores took an extra seven million shopper trips in the four weeks to 12 July 2026 against the same period last year, and branded soft drinks, confectionery and ice-cream were among the categories that picked up the benefit.”
More than a quarter of consumers (27%) say PMPs assure them they are paying a fair price, according to research group TWC. It adds that data gathered in August this year also indicates that 24% of consumers say PMPs make it easier for them to select a product.
However, TWC director Tom Fender, adds: “Suppliers have quite a difficult balancing act. They need to build in sufficient margin for the wholesaler as well as the retailer. Retailers’ cost of doing business is also rising and PMPs could be seen by some retailers as the supplier controlling margins.”
It is also acknowledged that not all retailers want PMPs. Fender says: “In some locations, the retailer could sell a product for higher than the price-mark. Also, stores open late at night or even 24 hours should be able to command a slightly higher price.”
Overall, however, PMPs are looked on favourably by retailers, as well as customers. Fender says: “PMPs play a vital role in helping convenience retailers to improve their price perception with frequent shoppers and new shoppers. Sixteen per cent of consumers agree with the statement ‘PMPs help me trust the retailer more’.”
Have your say

items.summary: Thousands of Poundland jobs and stores are at risk as the retailer has filed notice to appoint administrators. The move was prompted after the majority owners, Gordon Brothers, refused a solvent bid from Martin Property group, which increased the probability that the business could fall… This story continues at Poundland’s future hangs in the balance as it files for administration Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The move was prompted after the majority owners, Gordon Brothers, refused a solvent bid from Martin Property group, which increased the probability that the business could fall into administration.
The notice has been filed by the retail directors and, if approved by the High Court, will give the business 10 days’ breathing space to find a rescue deal.
Usdaw national officer Bally Auluk said: “It has been an incredibly distressing week for Poundland staff who have had to watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1.
“Poundland’s managing director Barry Williams has reluctantly filed a notice of intention, to give the business time to find a rescue deal and prevent Gordon Brothers from breaking up the business.
“We are urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider and to prioritise a unified buyer who will protect the livelihoods of 11,000 people.”
Sean Moran, insolvency partner at law firm Shakespeare Martineau, said: “It does seem counter intuitive that a discount store appears to be heading for administration as the country remains midst of a cost-of-living crisis.
“Poundland nevertheless faces the same challenges as other high street retailers with a combination of increases to the cost of its workforce and supply costs having ratcheted due to global conflicts whilst its customers are lured by better deals offered by competitors.
“Gordon Brothers has rolled the dice and will be hoping that the administration can achieve a more favourable outcome, perhaps through a pre-pack sale of all or part of the business, than trading on in its current guise.
“This will be tough news for the staff with many no doubt hoping for a rescue package via a pre-pack that will preserve some jobs.”

items.title: Certified reverse vending machines (RVMs) for deposit return scheme announced
items.summary: Exchange For Change, the industry-led organisation delivering the Deposit Return Scheme (DRS), has published the first list of certified Reverse Vending Machines (RVMs), supporting retailers as they prepare for the scheme’s launch on 1 October 2027. Certification confirms that a machine is compatible with the… This story continues at Certified reverse vending machines (RVMs) for deposit return scheme announced Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Certification confirms that a machine is compatible with the RVM specification required to operate within the scheme, having undergone rigorous testing and assessment to reach the certification standard.
Retailers considering purchasing or leasing an RVM are advised to check the approved list before selecting a model. The list will be updated on an ongoing basis as new RVMs are certified.
Certification of the RVMs has been undertaken by a specialist assessment provider tasked with independently conducting the full certification process, which will remain ongoing to allow for new RVM suppliers to submit their machines for assessment.
Certification assesses a range of technical and operational requirements to ensure machines can operate effectively within the DRS, including the identification and acceptance of eligible containers, fraud prevention, connectivity with scheme systems, accessibility requirements and the secure handling of transaction data.
Alongside the publication of the first certified machines, Exchange For Change has also published new RVM Artwork Guidance to support a consistent and recognisable approach across RVMs.
Russell Davies, Exchange For Change chief executive, said: “Publishing the first list of certified RVMs is an important step in helping retailers prepare for the launch of the Deposit Return Scheme in October 2027.
“Certification provides confidence that approved machines have met the requirements needed to operate within the scheme and gives retailers greater certainty as they consider their options.
“Retailers considering an RVM can now review the approved list and discuss the options available with suppliers. The list is designed to help retailers of all sizes make informed decisions ahead of the scheme launch, while the new Artwork Guidance provides retailers with approved branding that can be adopted alongside their own, helping to create a consistent and recognisable approach across the scheme.
“We will continue to provide guidance and support as preparations for scheme go-live progress, including through the grant scheme available to eligible small independent retailers to support the purchase of an RVM.”
The Federation of Independent Retailers (The Fed) has welcomed the publication of the list and said it follows close engagement between the Fed and Exchange for Change, coming after calls from its national president Hemanshu Patel to share key information with independent retailers as swiftly as possible, so they can fully engage with the scheme.
Patel said: “This is another important milestone in the roll-out of DRS, and the Fed will be monitoring this list closely so members wishing to install an RVM will be able to do so once the scheme goes live in less than a year’s time.
“The specification will also be critical for some of our members who will qualify for a £6,000 grant, with the application process launching in January 2027.
“We will continue to work closely with Exchange for Change to ensure that information is shared with our members, who will be crucial for ensuring DRS successfully boosts recycling in the years ahead.”
Travis Way, managing director at RVM specialists EcoVend, part of Reconomy, said: “The publication of the first certified reverse vending machine list gives retailers greater clarity as they prepare for the Deposit Return Scheme.
“With less than a year to go until launch, retailers should now be assessing their store footprint, considering how returns will fit into day-to-day operations and making sure staff are trained and ready to manage the process. Getting these practicalities in place early will be key to ensuring a smooth transition when the scheme goes live.
“A reliable, accessible network of return points will be key to encouraging participation, capturing more valuable materials for recycling and delivering the environmental benefits the scheme is designed to achieve.”

items.title: Poundland on brink of collapse as it files notice to appoint administrators
items.summary: Poundland is teetering on the edge of collapse after its directors filed a notice of intent to appoint administrators, in a move that puts the future of its thousands of workers in doubt. The company made the filing to the High Court on Thursday, suggesting that AlixPartners, its administrators, could be formally called in to [...]
items.body:
Poundland on brink of collapse as it files notice to appoint administrators
Poundland is teetering on the edge of collapse after its directors filed a notice of intent to appoint administrators, in a move that puts the future of its thousands of workers in doubt.
The company made the filing to the High Court on Thursday, suggesting that AlixPartners, its administrators, could be formally called in to take control of the business in the coming days. A collapse of Poundland could put nearly 12,000 jobs at risk and shutter its 640 stores in the UK and Ireland.
Poundland’s American owners Gordon Brothers had been considering a solvent takeover offer from Irish property firm Martin Property Group but have since rebuffed the bid in a dispute over a loan. Gordon Brothers wanted £30m to cover a shareholder loan despite inheriting it from Poundland’s previous owner Pepco when it bought the company for a nominal £1 last year.
This appointment of administrators has triggered a 10-day moratorium on the retailer’s creditors calling in their debts, allowing it a short window in which to save its stores and employees.
Should Poundland go under, it will throw scrutiny onto the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the sale process. Martin Property Group’s bid had been backed by Poundland’s management but the Irish company had refused to cover the £30m requested by Gordon Brothers, sources said.
Three new directors – who had been drafted in to accelerate the sale process – resigned earlier this week over Gordon Brother’s refusal to accept the bid.
Poundland’s collapse would deal a significant blow to Andy Burnham’s pledge to revive Britain’s high streets. The discount retailer is one of the country’s best-known high street brands and a fixture of town centres across the UK.
The Prime Minister will also be paying close attention to the future of Poundland’s distribution centre in Makerfield, his parliamentary constituency. Martin Property Group had promised to protect this site but its security would be far from secured if the retailer was broken apart.
Barry Williams, Poundland’s managing director, said on Thursday: “Despite enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole. The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs.
“We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment. We thank all stakeholders, and in particular our people for their support during this period.”
Burnham’s high street revival at risk
While Martin Property Group was the frontrunner to buy the entire Poundland business, a number of retailers have tabled bids for significant parts of the company’s sprawling 600-store estate.
These bidders have committed to taking on the staff at all the stores they acquire, according to Transfer of Undertakings (TUPE) rules, which aim to protect employees when a business changes hands.
Lidl, Iceland, The Range, B&M and Poundstretcher have all expressed interest in snapping up select stores if the company is broken up. These firms will be on the lookout for well-placed stores and some of Poundland’s stock. A break-up of the discount retailer could bring about the end of the Poundland brand.
The uncertain future of Poundland’s employees had already prompted stark warnings from Usdaw, the retail union, who branded Gordon Brothers an “absolute disgrace” and warned the retailer was teetering on the brink of administration.
Bally Auluk, the union’s national officer, said: “The owners’ failure to accept a solvent offer leads us to conclude they want to let the company fall into administration and make 11,000 people redundant in the run up to Christmas. I urge the Government to take robust action and save thousands of retail jobs.”
Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds wrote to Gordon Brothers this week to establish the facts of the situation, according to reports.

items.title: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback
items.summary: As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming CDs appear to be having a resurgence . John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, while another report on trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%. With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit. Continue reading...
items.body:
CDs appear to be having a resurgence. John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, while another report on trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%.
With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit.
‘I have well over 10,000 CDs’
Andrew Wales, 67, from London, owns “well over 10,000” CDs. “My wife’s very considerate,” he says over the phone. “There’s quite a few in this room where I’m speaking.” They have also spilt into the next bedroom and into the corridor.
“I don’t need Spotify,” says Wales. “The fact is, I like listening to music and I have always preferred owning it in a physical form. The [size of the] CD format allows me to own the number I own despite living in a two-bedroom flat and not a country mansion, so that’s another bonus.”
Much of the classical music Wales buys and listens to is available only on CD. “I bought my first CD in 1991 – John Scofield, Meant to Be – around the same time that I bought my first CD player. LPs were becoming increasingly shoddy, both in terms of pressing and presentation, and their limitations meant that often or not songs or tracks were included on the CD release, but not on LP. There are still cases where that happens today.”
That said, Wales also owns “about 2,000 LPs”, “a few hundred cassettes” and an increasing number of Blu-rays. “I’m not always wedded to a single format.”
‘After having a baby, our records were too bulky and inconvenient’
Unlike Wales, Gabriela Crowley, 32, from San Jose, California, started listening to CDs only over the last year. “Growing up, my parents had a tonne of them,” she says. “My dad played them in the car and everywhere. And then he got an iPod. By the time I was like 18, everything had started to shift away from physical media.”
Her return to physical records started with the vinyl trend a few years ago. “I met my husband, who also had a large record collection, and we enjoyed that hobby together for a while. But after having a baby, we found we really weren’t listening to our records much any more – they were too bulky and inconvenient. My father-in-law gave us one of his old CD players and now we use that every day.”
A CD collection helps with the “paradox of choice” that streaming brings, she says. “Instead of being paralysed by the endless options, you become more intimately familiar with what you have. I find it a much more satisfying way to engage with music. Plus, no autoplay or AI-generated playlists are being forced on me.”
‘I buy CDs directly from the bands’
“I bought my first CD in 1988 and have been collecting ever since,” says Neil Cumming, 53, from Gloucester. “I have several hundred of them. Everything from classical, folk, rock, blues …”
Cumming buys CDs mostly to support musicians. “I like a lot of small indie and folk bands, who are not making a lot of money. I buy CDs directly from them when I can, which means they get a bigger share of my money than they would if I streamed their music.
“And it means I own the CD for ever,” he says. “Streaming means you are basically renting the music, and it can disappear from the streaming sites. I enjoy the ritual of selecting a CD and putting it in the machine – it is a nicer experience than just pressing play on an app.”
Not that he’s anti-streaming. “It’s quite good for trying music before you buy CDs or finding new acts. But in the evening, with a mug of tea or a glass of whisky, I find the experience of a CD more satisfying.”
‘The antithesis of scrolling’
“I am drawn to the narrative and aesthetic arc of an album,” says Asha Varadharajan, 65, from Toronto. “It’s the antithesis of scrolling. I’ve never been a fan of music as white noise in the background, unless I’m boogying while vacuuming.”
Varadharajan has owned her CD player since 1999, “which allows me to listen to five CDs at a time in any order I choose, building my own narrative arc as I listen.
“I’m grateful to friends who introduced me to artists I may never have listened to,” she says. “The patience and persistence required in listening to a CD makes songs memorable. Streaming makes music ephemeral. I think algorithms make everything predictable, but everybody’s taste is kind of random.”
It helps that CDs are hard to damage, she says. “I’m a klutz and was terrified of scratching albums as a child because I never could place the needle accurately without my hand shaking.”
‘They give me something tactile and tangible’
Ed, 63, from London, bought his first CDs in 1986 – “Genesis, Invisible Touch, and Level 42, World Machine, if you must know” – and has “never stopped”, he says. “But my interest in the format has waxed and waned.
“When they first came out, CDs were very much positioned as: they’ll last for ever, you can drill holes in them, you can put jam on them and they still play. But I got put off CDs because they sounded too bright and shiny compared to vinyl.”
But over the past two years, Ed has bought more CDs owing to their “almost throwaway prices against the excessive costs of vinyl”. Having music on CD “gives me something tactile and tangible”, Ed says. “A good digital source is now every bit as engaging as a good record player.”

items.body:
The announcement also stated that SBRR would be lost for those who sell vapes though the Fed has received assurances that these will not apply to those as part of a much wider range of products.
However, the Fed plans to continue to engage closely with HMT and other government departments on how this and other changes relating to business rates will be rolled out.
The announcement was accompanied by confirmation of a further increase in the National Living Wage which the Fed commented on earlier on Wednesday and comes at a time a range of commercial costs like energy bills remain high.
Despite support for consumers and industrial companies with their energy bills, there was little extra support for small retailers struggling with higher energy costs.
The government has also maintained National Insurance Contributions for a higher rate and on earnings over £5,000 per annum, following a controversial tax change made in the budget two years ago.

“However, the message from the Fed remains that the cost of business remains too high. Our shops are crucial employers and also a familiar face in the communities they serve. It is important that the government continues to engage with the Fed to ensure that small retail businesses can survive.”
The Fed also welcomed measures announced in the budget to maintain the fuel duty cut of 5p per litre until July and a temporary reduction in import duties for a bundle of approximately 100 items often sold in independent convenience stores including baked beans and chocolate.

items.title: Gherkins and guffawing: Watching my first Budget, an idiot’s blow-by-blow account
items.summary: Culture writer Adam Bloodworth tried to watch the Budget 2026 in full. From the famous 4p off gherkins to the pantomime jibes, he struggled to keep pace with the childish politicians I am an alien in the City AM office. While the other journalists concern themselves with taxation and business rates, I am writing about [...]
items.body:
Gherkins and guffawing: Watching my first Budget, an idiot’s blow-by-blow account
Culture writer Adam Bloodworth tried to watch the Budget 2026 in full. From the famous 4p off gherkins to the pantomime jibes, he struggled to keep pace with the childish politicians
I am an alien in the City AM office. While the other journalists concern themselves with taxation and business rates, I am writing about theatre and restaurants. City AM’s tagline is ‘business with personality,’ and, humblebrag alert, I suppose I’m the personality.
By and large, politics and business is left off our pages – we like to take the reader away from their desks to somewhere more fabulous. And while important conversations take place over dinner, we’re concerned with telling you what to eat, where to go, and, crucially, who to put on the invite list.
And so it was new for me this year to sit through the entirety of the Budget – not just have it on in the background, but properly take it in. Here’s this lifestyle writer’s takeaways from the Autumn Budget 2026.
Call me a fish out of water, flailing desperately for validation in City AM’s hallowed towers.
Surely there was more to it than Kemi Badenoch’s take, that “the prime minister came in promising to reverse 40 years of neoliberalism. Instead we got 4p off gherkins?” Let’s see… I’m tuning in….
Budget 2026: I started with giant ambitions
I can take all this in. I can definitely take all this in. It’s basically an hour off work: watching a man deliver a speech about how he’s going to change the country. I have sat down, like millions of others across the nation, as a form of national service, to listen intently to this twice-annual sermon, only for the viewing experience to turn sour after about four-and-a-half minutes, when I had my first intrusive thought about pizza. It is, after all, lunchtime. All my hopes are quickly dashed. My mind wandering has caused me to lose the flow, and I’ve mucked this up, already. I thought I’d have at least 12 minutes in me. I can’t believe how quickly this has happened.
This isn’t going to work
This is too much information. Like, if ten minutes of someone talking fairly quickly without pausing feels like a lot of information, this is more than six times that. I really like Louis Theroux, but when I saw him say some fascinating things at How The Light Gets In festival this summer, I found myself thinking about pizza again. Sixty minutes is a long time. This is hopeless.
New approach
“You learn which bits to focus on!” my journo friend hollers from across the desk, shifting his headphones when he notices me in trouble. I can tell he’s half-zoned-out too, as he noticed me in the first place. This sounds good, and it kind of works. I tune in and have some Budget 2026 takeaways, like how “half of our shops, restaurants and gyms will pay no business rates at all”, but at other times it is still hopeless. By the time I’ve tuned back into the discourse, the Chancellor has sped ahead and moved onto something else. I feel useless, and dumb, like a stupid dumb baby.
Maybe that’s enough?
But I did learn something. I learned about founders’ relief and first time buyer ISAs and how we’re going to get 4p off gherkins, which loyal readers will know I’m very excited about. I did learn something. A lot, actually. Now I can relay this new skill to other life situations when friends bore me to tears tell me about their lives.
The pantomime stuff is so dumb
I know I’m the gazillionth person to say this, but how are ordinary people supposed to relate to the Budget 2026, and politics in general, when everyone in the Commons is literally making noises like a cow? Not to mention all the pointing and jeering, and making sassy comments. Deputy speaker Nursat Ghani told MPs they were behaving like their children, but she wasn’t much better, clapping back at one MP’s Budget rebuttal by telling him he’d “have to write yourself a prescription just to calm down”. It was one of a handful of panto villain remarks. She told another talkative MP: “I think you’ve spoken more words than the Chancellor during this statement.” It’s funny in the sense that Ghani has good comic timing, but tragic in that this Budget is affecting people’s lives and it seems like making cow noises and cracking jokes takes precedence over the politics.
The Budget 2026 is published online anyway
Don’t sweat it: everything’s published online, on the government website, minutes after the Budget 2026 speech is delivered in the Commons. So you can sit down and read it like a slow, wise old tortoise. I’d insert something here about how that’s what happens in politics anyway – everything takes forever and no one gets anything done, etcetera etcetera – but that would require me having taken in more of the Budget than I did, so I’ll just end this here. My head hurts.

The research, covering 730 self-checkouts in 100 London convenience stores run by four of the UK’s largest supermarket brands, found that on […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch!
