items.title: Why are online retailers being fined for unlawful sales tactics? Competition lawyer explains
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Charlie Markillie, partner in the Competition & Consumer Team at Knights, discusses what the recent fines issued to Wayfair, Appliances Direct and Gold’s Gym say about the Competition and Markets Authority’s growing focus on online sales practices, and what retailers should be reviewing now The Competition and Markets Authority’s (“CMA”) recent enforcement against Wayfair, Appliances […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Charlie Markillie, partner in the Competition & Consumer Team at Knights, discusses what the recent fines issued to Wayfair, Appliances Direct and Gold’s Gym say about the Competition and Markets Authority’s growing focus on online sales practices, and what retailers should be reviewing now
The Competition and Markets Authority’s (“CMA”) recent enforcement against Wayfair, Appliances Direct and Gold’s Gym is a warning to retailers: Online sales and pricing tactics are under more scrutiny than ever.
On the 14th October 2026, Wayfair was fined £4.8 million by the Competition and Markets Authority because it had falsely claimed some of its products were part of a ’24-hour flash sale’, despite them still being available at the same or lower price after the deal had ended. At the same time, Appliances Direct was fined £1.2 million for a similar issue relating to flash sale banners that falsely stated deals were limited, only for the same discount codes to keep reappearing over many days.
It’s a clear message from the regulator that it is paying close attention to practices designed to influence purchasing decisions.
Urgency claims are allowed, but not if they mislead
Countdown timers, flash sale messaging and popups are commonly used by retailers to encourage customers to act quickly on any purchases they’re considering. They are lawful provided they are accurate and don’t put unfair pressure on customers. When they cross the line into misleading consumers, the CMA can now act directly, and the penalties are significant.
Under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, the CMA can decide for itself that consumer law has been broken. It can then impose fines of up to 10% of a business’s global turnover without going to court. These cases are among the first to show those powers in use.
Automatic Opt-ins
As well as urgency claims, the CMA also investigated the use of pre-ticked paid extras by Appliances Direct, including ‘remove & recycle your old appliance’, and ‘installation on delivery’ services at checkout.
In its findings, the CMA said that customers must actively choose to pay for optional extras and can’t be signed up by default. On top of its fine, Appliances Direct must refund around £432,000 to affected customers. Their investigation wasn’t just limited to well-known brand names and businesses. Gold’s Gym, a franchise operating 4 UK fitness centres in London, advertised membership prices without including its joining fee, and didn’t make the fee sufficiently clear later in the purchasing journey either. It resulted in a £45,000 fine and the business was also already to pay refunds totalling £9,220 for 726 of its customers.
All three brands admitted the breaches and settled the cases early, earning them a 40% reduction on the fines imposed. Even so, the full cost goes well beyond the headline figures once refunds, legal costs and reputational damage are added.
The whole customer journey is in scope
The cases reflect the regulator’s growing willingness to use its enforcement powers against businesses that breach consumer law. The CMA is increasingly looking at the entire customer journey, from advertising and promotional activity through to checkout and final purchase.
One of the biggest challenges for online retailers is identifying where effective sales techniques end and misleading practices begin. Many of the practices under scrutiny are built into modern e-commerce platforms and marketing tools and are widely used across the sector, which may blur the lines further.
Retailers should ask not only “does this convert?” but also “could we defend this to the CMA?” Beyond the legal risks, people are becoming more savvy online and increasingly aware of misleading sales tactics and scams and can be quick to question businesses that lean too heavily on sales-driven messaging, whether intentional or not. Overstating the level of discount or imposing a false sense of urgency on consumers by using popups and timers can diminish credibility as a trusted business.
How retailers should respond
What retailers should do now
- Review recent promotions, especially those run outside major events such as Black Friday. Everyday “limited time” messaging is where the risk usually sits.
- Check what happened when promotions ended. Did prices actually change? Were banners and timers taken down?
- Switch off auto-repeat. Make sure urgency messaging and discount codes aren’t set to recycle automatically.
- Remove pre-ticked boxes for paid extras at checkout.
- Show the full price upfront, including any mandatory fees.
- Keep records that support your pricing and promotional claims, in case the CMA asks.
- Bring teams together. Marketing, e-commerce and compliance teams should all understand what the CMA treats as a concern.
Practices that have become commonplace across online retail are no longer escaping scrutiny. Retailers that review their promotions, pricing and checkout processes now will be in a far stronger position if the CMA comes knocking.

items.title: Nearly a third of children want to stay in education after getting a laptop, parents say
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Almost a third of parents (29%) found their child is more interested in going to college since getting a laptop, according to data from the Digital Poverty Alliance (DPA) and Currys. Two-thirds (65%) of parents also indicated their child was more motivated to do schoolwork, while 68% reported a rise in overall confidence after getting […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Almost a third of parents (29%) found their child is more interested in going to college since getting a laptop, according to data from the Digital Poverty Alliance (DPA) and Currys.
Two-thirds (65%) of parents also indicated their child was more motivated to do schoolwork, while 68% reported a rise in overall confidence after getting a laptop.
The findings come as nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training (NEETs), according to Alan Milburn’s review, with youth unemployment sitting at over 15%.
The Aspiration and Digital Inclusion report, published by the DPA and funded by Currys, surveyed teachers and participants in Tech4Families, a programme to help families experiencing digital exclusion. Its findings come as Alan Milburn prepares the final recommendations of his review into young people and work, having warned previously that fragmentation across education, welfare and employment makes it harder to identify young people at risk of becoming NEET.
The laptops provided to families enabled children to engage in schoolwork and homework, and in addition 69 per cent of parents said their children learnt new skills beyond education, such as how to apply for apprenticeships and work experience.
The share of children who could set up an email account doubled from 28% to 57%, while the share who could attach documents to an email rose from 29% to 59%, both of which are vital skills when applying for education courses, apprenticeships and jobs online.
Access to a laptop also had a significant impact for the wider household, with two-thirds of parents finding other family members making use of the device for work and job hunting. Over two-thirds (69%) said having a laptop changed how other family members see their own futures too, with parents updating CVs, applying for jobs and enrolling on courses. In almost one in five households where the laptop was shared, another family member used it to look for work.
“There are millions of children across the UK at a severe disadvantage, not just in education but in future job prospects, all because they do not have access to a laptop. Many of us take having a device for granted, but the reality is we’d feel lost without one. That’s what these children and families are facing each day, holding them back in school and their ability to apply for further education and work, which in turn impacts the job market and wider economy. Every child in the UK should have access to a keyboarded device, and that will require the government to launch a national digital schools census to understand the extent of the issue and reach the families most in need,” Elizabeth Anderson, CEO, Digital Poverty Alliance
“Today’s findings should be a wake-up call to us all. Too many young people across the UK are being held back by digital poverty, missing out on opportunities that many of us take for granted. At Currys, we want everyone to have equal access to the benefits of technology, especially when it is the gateway to education, employment, essential services and social connection. As this report reveals, access to tech doesn’t just help people get online – it can build confidence, raise aspirations and unlock opportunities. If we don’t act now, we risk leaving a generation behind,” said Moira Thomas, group sustainability & ESG director, Currys.

Available in 1.5kg packs, the range includes Six Seed Bread Flour, Cobber Bread Flour, Strong White Bread Flour, Mixed Grain Bread Flour, French Bread Flour and Wholemeal Bread Flour, alongside Pasta & Pizza Flour, […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Family-owned British flour brand Wessex Mill has secured a nine-strong listing at Ocado, bringing its award-winning range to the online supermarket.
Available in 1.5kg packs, the range includes Six Seed Bread Flour, Cobber Bread Flour, Strong White Bread Flour, Mixed Grain Bread Flour, French Bread Flour and Wholemeal Bread Flour, alongside Pasta & Pizza Flour, Plain White Flour and Self Raising Flour. The listing offers shoppers a broad choice of specialist and everyday flours, catering to a variety of home baking needs.
Owned by Michael and Clare Marriage, founders of Doves Farm Foods, Wessex Mill has a milling heritage spanning more than 125 years. Today, its flours are milled in the North Wessex Downs near Hungerford, where the business works closely with local farmers to source quality wheat from within 50 miles of the mill for its core range.
Combining generations of milling expertise with commitment to local sourcing, Wessex Mill slowly mills its wheat to produce high quality flour, with details of where the grain was grown printed on pack, giving shoppers greater visibility of the farms behind their flour.
Clare Marriage, co-owner of Wessex Mill, said: “We’re delighted to be bringing Wessex Mill to Ocado, making our flours more accessible to home bakers across the country. We’ve always believed that great baking starts with great flour, and knowing where your ingredients come from is an important part of that. From everyday favourites to specialist flours for artisan breads, pizza and pasta, we hope the range will inspire more people to get baking and experiment with different flours at home.”
The Wessex Mill range is available now at Ocado and from www.wessexmill.co.uk.
Range and pricing (1.5kg packs):
- Six Seed Bread Flour, RSP £3.20
- Cobber Bread Flour, RSP £3.20
- Strong White Bread Flour, RSP £2.30
- Mixed Grain Bread Flour, RSP £3.20
- French Bread Flour, RSP £3.20
- Wholemeal Bread Flour, RSP £2.30
- Pasta & Pizza Flour, RSP £3.70
- Plain White Flour, RSP £2.20
- Self Raising Flour, RSP £2.20
To support the listing, all nine flours will be available at Ocado with 20% off per pack for a limited period, from 4 November to 1 December 2026.

While Irish cream is a familiar favourite, Rogue takes a different approach, using cream sourced less than two miles from its […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Asda is turning up the indulgence this festive season with the launch of Rogue Irish Cream, a new liqueur made with fresh Irish dairy cream, triple-distilled Irish whiskey and rich vanilla and chocolate flavours.
While Irish cream is a familiar favourite, Rogue takes a different approach, using cream sourced less than two miles from its production site and bottled within 48 hours. For shoppers looking beyond the familiar names in the category, Rogue offers a new option at £10 for 1L, exclusively at Asda.
At the heart of Rogue is fresh cream from a family-run dairy in Inniskeen, Co. Monaghan, Ireland, home to around 100 Friesian cows. Delivered fresh each morning, the cream can go from cow to bottle in just 48 hours, bringing a distinctive freshness to the finished liqueur.
The cream is then blended with triple-distilled local Irish whiskey and grain neutral spirits, before being infused with vanilla, chocolate and a subtle hint of hazelnut to create a smooth, indulgent Irish cream.
And Rogue is just the beginning. Joining the original Irish Cream are two further Rogue flavours, a smooth Rogue Blonde and a Rogue Espresso Martini, giving shoppers even more ways to enjoy the range over the festive season.
Rogue is available on Asda.com now: https://www.asda.com/groceries/product/baileys-rogue-cream-liqueurs/rogue-irish-cream-liqueur-1-litre/9405661

items.summary: Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. items.body:
In John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax? Ruled out. A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m? Off the table. Even the briefed increase in the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it was until the Conservatives cut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air.
Poll after poll shows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – including three in five Reform-leaning voters. We know that wealth inequality – with the richest 50 families in the UK possessing more wealth than half of the UK population – is weakening our economy, eroding our social fabric and undermining our democracy. Just last year, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, explicitly acknowledged that we have “overtaxed labour and undertaxed wealth”. So what on earth is going on?
To solve this paradox, our team at Tax Justice UK joined forces with researchers at the University of Strathclyde to go straight to the source. We interviewed 30 politicians across Westminster, Holyrood and the Senedd between February and July 2026, while Keir Starmer was prime minister. We made sure, in particular, that we spoke to every faction of the Labour party in Westminster – as the party in government and the party we would expect to be predisposed to higher taxes on the super-rich, its opinions inevitably garner more interest. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the hidden machinery of British politics. They suggest that the barrier to taxing extreme wealth is a deeply entrenched pattern of political fear, economic uncertainty, institutional capture and parliamentary self-preservation. And while these interviews took place under the former leadership, our conversations with MPs since suggest that, unless Burnham commits to higher taxes on wealth, the same barriers do hold.
The problem doesn’t start in parliament. Far from the green benches, a hostile climate is carefully cultivated to make taxing wealth seem undesirable. A billionaire-owned media apparatus relentlessly pushes scare stories, successfully tricking ordinary homeowners into thinking a “wealth tax” targets their modest family homes rather than offshore holdings and multimillion-pound assets. Outlets constantly tell us that billionaires are leaving the UK because of new taxes – even those who actually left a decade ago – and quote “millionaire flight” figures from a seriously flawed report. It doesn’t matter if they are not true – these narratives successfully penetrate the hearts and minds of parliamentarians.
Whether MPs are dismissing the prospect because they assume that the public would never go for it, not wanting to face the press backlash, or wanting stronger empirical proof covering every micro-detail of policy design and its potential impacts, this media backdrop directly undermines politicians’ confidence in fighting for higher taxes on wealth. Demands for evidence are reasonable, of course – yet we rarely see this scrutiny applied to spending on defence or AI.
Then there is the direct influence of elite money. There is a perception that when you are rich enough, you don’t need to shout from the public gallery: you have elite access. As one Labour politician told us: “If the City doesn’t like it then sometimes it can change views here in a way that’s not helpful.”
Inside parliament, this structural pressure transforms into personal paralysis. Even backbenchers who privately champion wealth taxes often won’t stick their necks out ahead of party leaders. One Labour MP confessed to keeping quiet for fear of losing local funding, admitting: “I’m trying not to be an out-and-out rebel, because I want another Pride in Place award for a really deprived part of my constituency.”
When constituency improvements are held hostage to party-line conformity, acting on principle becomes complicated. Yet this dynamic also reveals an opportunity: our interviews revealed that if the party leadership took a decisive stand on taxing wealth, most Labour MPs would fall in line behind it. Furthermore, given that Burnham has been far warmer towards higher taxes on wealth than Starmer – who notoriously referred to wealth tax campaigners as “snake oil merchants” – there is potentially more space and opportunity for MPs to speak up.
For the PM himself, this may or may not be an issue he is willing to be brave on. The danger, of course, is that the view looks very different from the inside. The retreat we are seeing suggests that Burnham and his team are already succumbing to the very same Westminster pressures our research laid bare.
One might assume that underlying some of this political resistance is an ideological dogma that taxing extreme fortunes somehow “punishes success”. But while we encountered this view among interviewees on the political right, we found little evidence of it elsewhere. Which perhaps is some cause for celebration: if many of the barriers are not ideological, there are practical things we can do.
First, we would do well to remember that winning the argument on wealth taxation isn’t just a policy battle – it’s a narrative one. As several interviewed politicians noted, the movement for economic justice must stop focusing too heavily on “who pays”, and start relentlessly highlighting “what the money buys”. People are far less interested in taxing billionaires than they are in fixing their local NHS hospitals, repairing crumbling schools and investing in green infrastructure. Taxing wealth must be framed positively as a seed investment in collective prosperity. Positive, gain-focused messaging strips away the weaponised narrative that tax is inherently bad.
Ultimately, our research reminds us that civil society cannot sit back and wait for a progressive frontbench to deliver change from above. The structural incentives inside parliament are designed to manufacture caution, not courage.
Until we make it more dangerous for politicians to ignore the public than to challenge the super-rich, we will continue to get budgets that fail to correct a fundamental unfairness at the heart of our tax system. The polls show the country is already with us. Now we must translate that quiet consent into unshakeable public pressure to push on the door left ajar by Burnham’s previously stated positions. Just like wealth, true reform has never trickled down from the top – it is built from the ground up.
- Faiza Shaheen is executive director of Tax Justice UK

items.title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
items.summary: Figures obtained by BBC Newsnight show large spikes in sales of torches, radios and power banks.
items.body:
Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
- Published
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.
The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.
The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.
Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.
The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.
"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.
"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."
On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.
Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.
In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."
An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."
Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.
Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing â order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."
Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

items.title: ETAM teams with commercetools to modernise digital retail foundation supporting brands including Maison 123
items.summary: commercetools has announced a partnership with French fashion retailer ETAM Group that aims to modernise its digital commerce and accelerate innovation across brands like ETAM, Maison 123 and Undiz.The tie up follows an eight-week MVP developed by ETAM's Digital Factory in early 2026 to demonstrate
items.body:
commercetools has announced a partnership with French fashion retailer ETAM Group that aims to modernise its digital commerce and accelerate innovation across brands like ETAM, Maison 123 and Undiz.
The tie up follows an eight-week MVP developed by ETAM's Digital Factory in early 2026 to demonstrate the potential of a modern, flexible commerce architecture against its existing environment.
Built on commercetools Sphere, with support from Algolia and Contentstack, the MVP demonstrated a 70–80% increase in development velocity, according to those involved.
"From the outset, our work with commercetools has been about more than replacing technology. We're building a commerce foundation that gives our teams greater speed and our brands more freedom to innovate," says Sébastien Ribeil, Head of Digital Factory at ETAM Group.
"The progress we made together in just eight weeks demonstrated what this approach can unlock, significantly increasing development velocity and giving us a way forward in how we can continue to evolve and grow. Just as importantly, it opens the door to new omnichannel experiences, a strategic priority for ETAM Group in the years ahead."
ETAM is now replacing its legacy commerce platform with commercetools. The API native architecture will integrate with ETAM's existing IT ecosystem while enabling individual capabilities to evolve independently, with the aim of giving its brands greater autonomy while maintaining a shared commerce foundation.
“ETAM approached this transformation in exactly the way we believe modern commerce should be built: prove the value quickly, give the people closest to the business the ability to build, and create an architecture that can keep changing with them,” says Dirk Hoerig, Founder and Chief Innovation Officer at commercetools.
“What we're building together isn't simply a replacement for ETAM's existing platform. It's a foundation that gives its teams and brands the freedom to move faster today, while preparing the business for the much bigger changes AI will bring to commerce.”
The Digital Factory used AI assisted development during the MVP to accelerate delivery with its existing engineering team. ETAM says it will continue to explore how AI can improve engineering productivity and reduce manual development effort, while commercetools Sphere enables the introduction of new AI powered commerce capabilities as they emerge.
Over time, this will support ETAM as it expands into new markets, introduces new capabilities and adapts its commerce strategy as customer expectations and technology continue to evolve.

When I made this choice a few months back, it came down to a personal decision to relocate from t
items.body:
Jayesh Bhayani has left Tesco, where he spent the past ten years and served as Chief Product and Technology Officer.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: "A couple of weeks ago, I officially retired from Tesco. When I made this choice a few months back, it came down to a personal decision to relocate from the UK, rather than a desire to leave Tesco."
"While there is quite a lot to say about commercial milestones, transformation metrics, and deliveries, I would rather focus on what actually drives an organisation of this magnitude - its culture."
He added: "Tesco is fundamentally built on great individuals and team-ship across the business. It remains one of the most authentically people-centric companies I have ever encountered. It is incredibly rare to find an enterprise operating at this massive scale that still maintains such genuine support for its colleagues. The culture here runs deep."
"To everyone across the business I have had the privilege of working alongside over the last decade, ‘Thank You’. You have made these past ten years an exceptional chapter of my life and contributed immensely to my own personal growth. I wish you my very best for the future."

items.title: Scottish retailer House of Bruar connects with Yocuda for introduction of digital receipts in stores
items.summary: House of Bruar, a Scottish luxury country lifestyle department store, says it has boosted its in-store customer experience with digital receipts in partnership with Yocuda.﻿Despite initial concerns regarding its mature customer base - the largest visitor age group is 55 to 64 years old - shoppers ha
items.body:
House of Bruar, a Scottish luxury country lifestyle department store, says it has boosted its in-store customer experience with digital receipts in partnership with Yocuda.
Despite initial concerns regarding its mature customer base - the largest visitor age group is 55 to 64 years old - shoppers have actively interacted with the new digital channel.
Highlights: digital receipts achieved a 70% open rate, over four times the standard retail marketing email benchmark of 17%; click-through rates reached 6% - nearly nine times the retail industry average of 0.7% - driving store shoppers back to online catalogues, product recommendations, and brand content; shoppers can send paperless gift receipts with personalised messages directly from their own digital receipt, thereby enabling House of Bruar to encourage gift recipients to sign up to its CRM.
Before implementing Yocuda, House of Bruar had limited visibility into purchasing habits in its physical store.
"Digital receipts have been a valuable addition to the in-store customer journey, giving customers a convenient, paperless way to keep track of their purchases while also creating another touchpoint with House of Bruar," says Ali Black, Head of Retail at House of Bruar.
"While some customers may choose to continue their journey online rather than return to store, this still benefits the business by keeping customers engaged with the wider brand and making it easier for them to shop across both our physical and online channels."
“As we run a legacy PoS, integration was the part of the project we expected to be most difficult. In practice, Yocuda worked around our existing setup, built and tested the integration on our test PoS, and we went from project start to live across all tills in just a few weeks, without needing a third-party integrator and with very little demand on our internal team," says Iain Jackson, Head of IT.
"Digital receipts have helped us bridge the data gap between our in-store and online customers, giving us greater visibility of customers who previously may only have interacted with us in-store," says John Hodge, Head of E-commerce and Mail Order.
"This has allowed us to better connect their online and offline journeys, build a more recognised picture of customer behaviour and, importantly, continue engaging with them beyond their visit to House of Bruar."

items.title: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises
items.summary: British Retail Consortium says ‘dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs’ being kept from consumers Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers. The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out. Continue reading...
items.body:
Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.
The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.
It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.
Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.
The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.
Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.
Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”
She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.
The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.
The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.
Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.
Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project working in partnership with over 200 hundred families.
She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants surveyed for the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.
One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”
The report involves responses from 76 participants, of which 73 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.
“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

items.body:
American Express and Home Bargains have signed a new agreement meaning Amex is now accepted as a payment method both in-person and online at one of the UK’s leading discount retailers.
Since being founded in 1976 in Liverpool, Home Bargains has grown to become one of the largest privately-owned companies in the UK, now operating over 650 stores nationwide, and employing more than 29,000 colleagues.
The discount store chain specialises in offering value pricing on high street brands including household goods, health and beauty, toys and food.
Promotion of the new acceptance agreement will include targeted email communications to Amex Cardmembers, digital marketing, and social media activity.
Home Bargains joins a record number of businesses in the UK – including every major supermarket chain, most high street retailers and more small businesses than ever before – that recognise the value of welcoming Amex Cardmembers – who are typically higher spending than other credit card users.
Dan Edelman, UK general manager, merchant services at American Express, said: “We are committed to ensuring our Cardmembers can use their Card wherever they live, work and travel. We’re delighted that American Express is now accepted by Home Bargains, one of the UK’s fastest-growing retailers. This agreement reinforces our strong merchant coverage nationwide, which has tripled since 2021.”
Phil Hoad, group finance director at Home Bargains, said: “We’re delighted to now accept American Express both in our stores and online, giving customers even more choice and convenience when shopping with Home Bargains. We know many of our customers value the flexibility that American Express provides, and we’re pleased to make it easier for them to pay in the way that suits them best while continuing to offer the top brands at bottom prices they’re used to.”
American Express provides Cardmembers with a range of benefits including cashback, Membership Rewards® points, exclusive Amex Offers from national brands, and more. In the UK, American Express is accepted at more places than ever before, meaning there is a greater choice of businesses where Cardmembers can earn rewards when paying with Amex.
In the UK since 2021, the number of locations accepting American Express has tripled, including more UK small businesses than ever before. American Express Cards are accepted at over 170 million merchant locations worldwide as of year-end 2025.2

Running from 26th October – 31st October, customers can simply enter the game through the More Card app every day to win a variety of prizes, ranging from free products and store discounts to a jackpot of up to one million More Points, worth £1,000.
The Halloween-themed game follows the success of Morrisons Easter Mix & Match Countdown earlier this year, giving customers another fun and interactive way to make the most of their More Card membership, with a spooky seasonal twist.
Gareth Lloyd, marketing director for Value and Loyalty at Morrisons, said: “Halloween is all about surprises, so we wanted to bring a little of that magic to our More Card members this October. Aldi is set to open seven new stores in just one month, creating up to 210 jobs across the UK.
The supermarket will open seven stores across England throughout November, including two new locations in London, with up to 30 roles available at each site.
The openings form part of Aldi’s £370 million investment in its UK estate this year, as it works towards its long-term ambition of operating 1,500 stores nationwide.
It comes after Aldi unveiled plans for further store investment, continued price cuts and more long-term agreements with British suppliers in its annual trading update earlier this month.
Jonathan Neale, managing director of national real estate at Aldi UK, said: “Demand for new Aldi stores remains strong, and we want more shoppers to be able to enjoy our high-quality products at low prices.
“Opening seven stores in November is another big step in our growth plans. It will create hundreds of local jobs and bring Aldi’s value to thousands more shoppers across the country.”
The Aldi stores opening in November are:
- Basildon, Essex – 12th November
- Newport, Isle of Wight – 19th November
- Matlock, Derbyshire – 19th November
- Stepney Green, London – 19th November
- Willesden, London – 26th November
- Orrell, Wigan – 26th November

The firm has insisted loans will have “transparent terms” and [...]
items.body:
Revolut to take fight to high street banks with UK personal loans
Revolut is ramping up its battle with high street banking giants with the launch of personal loans in the UK market.
The digital bank said on Monday it would begin offering loans between £2,000 and £25,000, which will be repayable over one to five years.
The firm has insisted loans will have “transparent terms” and funds will be transferred within “minutes” following approval.
“UK consumers can face unnecessary friction and complex fee structures when borrowing. We’ve built a transparent and simple loan process with near-instant funds on approval, no fee for early repayment and competitive rates,” Francesca Carlesi, chief executive of Revolut UK, said.
Rates will range from 6.9 per cent to 29.3 per cent APR.
Carlesi added bringing credit into the group’s ecosystem would help customers use its product for an “all in one place” experience.
The move will push Revolut beyond its foundational payment products and put it toe-to-toe with incumbent lenders.
Revolut eyes competitive mortgage market
Revolut was created in 2015 and has expanded across lifestyle and payment products. Earlier this year, it secured its full-fat UK banking licence after a four-year wait paving the way for it to enter the riskier market of lending.
Carlesi told Reuters the firm plans to eventually enter the UK’s competitive mortgage market. Lloyds Banking Group currently dominates the mortgage market, owning roughly a fifth of the market share. But it also faces competition from the likes of Natwest, Santander, Barclays and the country’s largest building society Nationwide.
The UK’s big four banks – Natwest, Lloyds, HSBC and Barclays – currently hold around 60 per cent of the industry’s £2.5 trillion in deposits.
Revolut, which boasts 80m customers globally and 13m in the UK, posted a 57 per cent surge in group-wide profit to £1.7bn in its latest financial year, driven by growth across subscriptions, payments and wealth.
Subscriptions notched the highest year-on-year revenue increase – and outperformed headline profit and revenue growth – at 67 per cent to £708m.
But its per-customer revenue has remained below rivals as the firm continues to fight for users to use the service as their primary bank.
Revolut’s founder Nik Storonsky said in March following the licence approval that launching the UK bank had been a “long-term strategic priority.. and marks a significant moment in our journey”.

items.title: UK retailers prepare for Halloween horror as shoplifting looks set to hit 2.5 times 2025 levels
items.summary: With Halloween landing on Saturday this year, SAI is warning UK retailers that theft incidents could rise as much as 2.5 times the level experienced in 2025.While Halloween is now one of the biggest sales events of the UK retail calendar, heightened footfall in-store alongside ongoing economic press
items.body:
With Halloween landing on Saturday this year, SAI is warning UK retailers that theft incidents could rise as much as 2.5 times the level experienced in 2025.
While Halloween is now one of the biggest sales events of the UK retail calendar, heightened footfall in-store alongside ongoing economic pressures on household finances mean the spooky season has become a growing target for theft.
Data from SAI's One Platform, which analyses insight from more than 1,000 UK retail locations and inputs from over 30,000 cameras every day, showed that in 2025 Halloween (Friday, 31st Oct) shoplifting rose by +67% on the daily average.
This year, with Halloween falling on a Saturday - consistently one of the highest risk days of the week for retail crime - shoplifting is forecast to rise 150% year-on-year.
Partial payment is expected to make up the majority of shoplifting attempts (58%). This is followed by grab and go theft (33%) and item switching, where a shopper deliberately selects a lower priced product at self-checkout in place of a higher value item (8%).
“Often regarded as the gateway to the Golden Quarter, Halloween provides retailers with an early opportunity to kick off their Peak Trading campaigns. But with that potential reward comes risk, and the darker side of Halloween is becoming a growing challenge for retailers wanting to capitalise on seasonal spending,” says Clare Hoole, Head of UK at SAI.
She adds: “Surges in footfall, combined with colleagues focused on servicing busier stores, can create more opportunities for theft, while more sophisticated offending behaviours, such as partial payment, become harder to detect."
"Real-time visibility and intelligence that enable retailers to intervene before losses occur will be critical to protecting margins and delivering a successful Spooky Season trading period.”
Looking ahead to the rest of the Golden Quarter, SAI forecasts that Super Saturday (19th December), the last Saturday before Christmas and often one of the busiest in-store trading days of the festive season, will be the biggest day for retail crime, with shoplifting expected to surge +66% year-on-year.

items.body:
At around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare.
Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience. He filled his store with dazzling window displays, world-class entertainment, restaurants and lounges. He even installed women’s toilets – a rarity in Edwardian England – giving women a newfound freedom to make the most of the city. As he opened the doors to his first customers, he told them “everyone is welcome”.
That spirit has been at the heart of Oxford Street’s success ever since. We love it because it feels as if it belongs to all of us. It’s where teenagers come for their first shopping trip with friends. Where families marvel at the magic of festive lights and decorations. And where generations of Londoners and visitors have come to discover the latest music, fashion and trends. It’s also the beating heart of British retail – pumping billions into our national economy, with the surrounding area accounting for an incredible 1% of the UK’s total economic output in 2022.
But in recent years this iconic street has started to lose some of its sparkle. Changing consumer habits and the legacy of the pandemic have taken their toll. Footfall has fallen. Some of our best-loved stores have closed their doors, only to be replaced by vape shops and candy stores. And, too often, the experience of visiting a chaotic, congested Oxford Street has felt more like an ordeal to survive than a day out to enjoy.
If we’re to restore this beloved street to its former glory, we must rediscover the pioneering spirit of Harry Gordon Selfridge and create a space for everyone to enjoy, breathing new life into the high street and bringing back big brands. And that’s what our bold plans – backed by the overwhelming majority of Londoners and businesses – are all about. And with household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks investing in new stores, there’s already excitement for what Oxford Street can become.
People need a reason beyond simply buying something to visit their high street. And in an age when almost anything can be delivered right to our door, that principle matters more than ever. Coming to Oxford Street should feel like a positive experience. Somewhere you want to spend time, as well as your hard-earned money. A place where you’re not choked by tailpipe fumes or deafened by the noise of passing motorists. And that starts with reclaiming it for pedestrians, not traffic – rebalancing the relationship between cars and people in the centre of our city.
That’s why I’m so delighted that, thanks to our efforts, the road stretching between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is now officially traffic-free. But removing cars is just the beginning. Imagine an Oxford Street where you can stroll at your own pace, take a break from shopping with a coffee under the trees, or stumble across some live music, a fashion show, a sports exhibition or a cultural event. We’re determined to put Oxford Street not just on par with top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla, but make it even better.
And while it’s a process – we’re deliberately keeping disruption to a minimum over the busy Christmas period – by next spring, visitors can expect to see new trees, new seats and new public plazas, alongside improved lighting and signage. This ambitious project has been far from straightforward or easy. As usual, we’ve had to overcome opposition from a vocal minority, and 14 years of a previous government that didn’t back the plans. But with seven in 10 Londoners expressing support for our vision, after extensive consultation, I knew we owed it to our city and to our businesses to deliver these improvements, which will help to boost jobs, growth and investment as we build a fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.
Of course, we’ll continue to listen to Londoners. Many of the initial changes are temporary, and we’ll use real-time feedback to help refine the final designs in a test and review period throughout 2027. But for centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way. And now it’s in need of its next great transformation. One that honours its extraordinary past while creating new possibilities for the future. A future where new memories are made, new businesses flourish and new chapters of British history are written.
Today marks the beginning of that journey – and I encourage everyone to come to explore this newly transformed street, as we work together to ensure its best days are still to come. In the words of Harry Gordon Selfridge – everyone is welcome.
- Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

items.summary: Morrisons is among the finalists at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards, with this year's winners being announced at an event in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.It has been shortlisted for initiatives encompassing several major technological upgrades to enhance its shopping experience. items.body:
Morrisons is among the finalists at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards, with this year's winners being announced at an event in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
It has been shortlisted for initiatives encompassing several major technological upgrades to enhance its shopping experience. Firstly, it is trialling AI powered Caper Carts from Instacart for an autonomous checkout process.
Secondly, it deployed digital Bluetooth probing across its Oven Fresh departments to automate food safety checks. The UK grocery retailer rolled out a Pick to Light system using digital shelf edge labels to guide online pickers.
Finally, its Everseen roll-out has supported front end efficiency and made improvements into loss recovery. Together, these innovations are driving efficiency, boosting performance, and transforming retail operations.
For the Caper Carts project, Morrisons built a bespoke, interim integration bridge to align the technology with legacy systems before its new Emerald PoS roll-out. Similarly, its Everseen roll-out created an integration between numerous technology systems before a full operational reset and training process to support.
For the digital Bluetooth probing initiative, all 475 Oven Fresh counters transitioned to continuous temperature monitoring and instant alarm triggers; allowing Morrisons to improve merchandising guidelines. Pick to Light was rolled out to 200 stores and this is continuing, creating an increase in UPH supported by deploying regional specialists to demonstrate execution standards.

lululemon has announced the addition of Shopify's Shop Pay solution to its Canada and US e-commerce sites.

items.title: Fashion retailer Gap Inc. starts scaling Bridgette, an AI tool for seasonal hiring, across stores and DCs
items.summary: Gap Inc. has started to scale Bridgette, an AI enabled virtual career guide for seasonal hiring, across its stores and distribution centres.Bridgette answers candidate questions at any hour, coordinates interviews and sends reminders. In a pilot, nearly 45,000 candidates engaged with it, and it has
items.body:
Gap Inc. has started to scale Bridgette, an AI enabled virtual career guide for seasonal hiring, across its stores and distribution centres.
Bridgette answers candidate questions at any hour, coordinates interviews and sends reminders. In a pilot, nearly 45,000 candidates engaged with it, and it has scheduled more than 7,000 interviews for store leaders.
In a LinkedIn post, Sven Gerjets, EVP and CTO at Gap Inc., said: "It works every day of the week, which is a better schedule than mine. What I care about most is what it does not do. Managers still run the interviews and make the hiring decisions. That is the point."
He added: "Our approach to AI is human centered and digitally enabled. For every step in a process, we ask what should be automated, what should be AI assisted, and what should stay with a person. Then we redesign the work around the outcome instead of speeding up the old process."
"Hiring is a good example, because the repetitive coordination was crowding out the conversations that build great teams. I keep coming back to a simple test. Does the technology give people their time back for the human work that matters most?"

items.title: Debenhams Group returns to Burnley in fulfilment operations partnership with GXO Logistics
items.summary: Debenhams Group, home to Debenhams, PrettyLittleThing, boohoo, MAN and Karen Millen, has announced plans to move its fulfilment operations back to Burnley, through a new global distribution partnership with GXO Logistics. The move is expected to create over 1,200 jobs.Dan Finley, CEO at Debenhams Gr
items.body:
Debenhams Group, home to Debenhams, PrettyLittleThing, boohoo, MAN and Karen Millen, has announced plans to move its fulfilment operations back to Burnley, through a new global distribution partnership with GXO Logistics. The move is expected to create over 1,200 jobs.
Dan Finley, CEO at Debenhams Group, says: “We’re delighted to be returning to Burnley. Burnley has played an important role in the group’s history, as the primary distribution location for over a decade. We’re excited to be combining our years of experience operating in the town with GXO’s fulfilment expertise, to support the next phase of the group’s growth."
In September, the group announced the £90 million sale of its Sheffield distribution centre to Primark. Debenhams Group expects to continue operating from Sheffield until early 2027, ahead of the transfer to Burnley. GXO will run the Burnley facility under a new agreement to oversee Debenhams Group’s global third-party distribution.
Russell Atkinson, Managing Director of Fashion and Apparel, GXO UK&I, says: “We’re excited to begin this new partnership with Debenhams, bringing GXO’s retail logistics expertise and global network to support its continued growth.”
Oliver Ryan, MP for Burnley, Padiham and Brierfield, says: "This is great news for Burnley and another vote of confidence in our town. The move will deliver jobs, apprenticeships and huge economic benefits in the years ahead. Debenhams Group have gone through a strong turnaround, and I'm glad to have them back as a local partner."
