items.title: Sensei gets physical in Brazil and Co-op turns data into action: last week’s biggest retail technology plays
items.summary: RTIH rounds up the stand out retail technology deals, launches, deployments and pilots from the past seven days. Including Coles Group, Coveo, Circana, Ocado Group, AiFi, Primark, Brompton, Commerce, Old Spike, Square, Debenhams Group, Booker Wholesale, and Samsung Electronics.Coles GroupColes Group
items.body:
RTIH rounds up the stand out retail technology deals, launches, deployments and pilots from the past seven days. Including Coles Group, Coveo, Circana, Ocado Group, AiFi, Primark, Brompton, Commerce, Old Spike, Square, Debenhams Group, Booker Wholesale, and Samsung Electronics.
Coles Group
Coles Group has selected Coveo to power AI search and product discovery on coles.com.au.
"We're always looking for ways to make shopping with Coles easier for our customers, and search is an important part of the online experience," says Ben Levinson, General Manager of Digital Product at Coles. "Coveo demonstrated that its technology will make it easier for customers to find the products they are looking for, and we look forward to continuing to improve the Coles online shopping experience."
"Helping Australians find their everyday grocery products faster and easier is a great opportunity for Coveo" says Alexander Mahr, Managing Director, APAC, at Coveo. "We're proud to support Coles as it creates a smarter, more intuitive online grocery experience for customers across Australia."
RV@Olympic
AiFi has partnered with RV@Olympic camp site and resort in Port Angeles, Washington, USA on the launch of a checkout free store.
In a LinkedIn post, AiFi said: "It’s 9 PM near Olympic National Park and you’ve just realised you’re out of snacks for tomorrow’s 6am hike. Most campground stores closed hours ago. At RV@Olympic in Port Angeles, Washington, guests can still walk over and get some."
It added: "We’ve partnered with RV to open the first fully autonomous campground store in the United States. Guests walk in, take what they need, and leave. AiFi’s spatial intelligence platform handles checkout in real time, so nobody has to staff a register overnight."
"A staffed store here would run 9am to 5pm. Today, 56.6% of the store’s revenue comes in outside those hours. A store that closes at 5pm sends most of that demand back to the campsite empty-handed."
Co-op
Circana and Co-op have announced a new multi-year agreement, extending a partnership that launched in 2020.
Over the past few years, the former's HIVE portal has become a key part of Co-op’s data strategy, enabling the retailer and its suppliers to work from the same data and build a shared understanding of customer behaviour, category performance and market trends.
HIVE brings together EPoS transactions, shopper insights, loyalty metrics, purchasing behaviours and market performance to provide a single view of performance across the business.
The renewed agreement marks the next phase of HIVE’s development, with the aim of strengthening Co-op’s ability to unlock value from its data assets while helping suppliers make faster, more informed decisions.
Over the next five years, Circana and Co-op will expand the platform’s capabilities through the integration of new data assets and measurement solutions, including supply chain, quick commerce and wholesale insights.
Imran Rasul, Chief Commercial Officer, Co-op, says: “We are delighted to deepen and extend our relationship with Circana. The next evolution of HIVE will provide suppliers with broader, more connected insights across our business, enabling faster decision-making, stronger collaboration and greater opportunities for shared growth. Together, we're creating a platform that helps turn data into action and supports long-term success for both Co-op and its partners.”
Ocado Group and AEON
Ocado Group and AEON have announced the official go live of their second customer fulfilment centre (CFC) in Japan. The facility in Hachioji City, Tokyo was unveiled by AEON executives at a ceremony at the site.
This will provide additional capacity to enable the growth of AEON’s Green Beans online grocery delivery brand across the Tokyo region, as well as driving logistical efficiency and shorter delivery distances across its network. Hachioji is the second Ocado CFC to use its Auto-Freezer system following the recent launch of Lotte's CFC in Busan, South Korea.
This uses a specialised version of Ocado’s fulfilment bot to process frozen orders 2.7 times faster than AEON’s first CFC in Chiba, and increases freezer inventory capacity by 150% while reducing the required storage footprint by 50%. The Auto-Freezer will also reduce the time spent by staff in freezer conditions to below 5% of their working hours.
The four-storey CFC has a gross floor area of approximately 40,000 m², and is equipped with a full suite of Ocado’s Re:Imagined technologies, including On-Grid Robotic Pick. The site will also offer a Pickup service, allowing customers to collect orders directly from the site in as little as three hours.
Sam's Club
Affirm has announced an exclusive, multi-year tie up with Sam’s Club that will give eligible shoppers a buy now, pay later option. Affirm will be available on SamsClub.com in the coming weeks, with plans afoot to expand availability to Sam’s Club locations in 2027.
“Making every dollar count shouldn’t stop at checkout,” says Wayne Pommen, CRO at Affirm. “When people pay over time with Affirm, they know what they’ll owe and choose a plan that fits their lives. That way, every dollar counts after checkout, too.”
At checkout, shoppers will complete a quick, real-time eligibility check for purchases. If approved, they can choose a monthly plan and see each payment and exactly when they’ll be done before they commit. Affirm says that it never charges late fees, and interest never compounds.
Fran's Chocolates
Fran's Chocolates, a US-based gourmet chocolatier, is among the first customers worldwide to test Aviator, Avalara's newly unveiled agent hub for tax and compliance.
For years, Fran's Chocolates had little reason to worry about multistate sales tax compliance. That changed as the company's e-commerce and wholesale businesses grew across the country and the Wayfair decision expanded states' authority to enforce economic nexus rules.
The company implemented Avalara AvaTax to automate tax calculations across jurisdictions, Managed Returns to handle filing and remittance, and Exemption Certificate Management (ECM) to track and validate exemption certificates.
Fran's Chocolates says it reduced reliance on additional full-time employees, saving up to $120,000 annually in salary and benefits, and reclaimed more than 100 hours a year by automating tax classification across a catalogue of more than 900 SKUs, including the 40 to 60 new products it typically introduces annually. Automated, jurisdiction specific tax reporting has also helped shorten its financial close cycles.
"Economic nexus rules are always changing, and keeping up with them used to mean hours of manual cross-checking," says Ken Harrison, Senior Accountant at Fran's Chocolates. "Avalara helps us see where we're approaching nexus before it becomes a problem, and recently using Avalara Aviator has shown us how much further that early warning can go. The agent does the scanning, and we decide what to act on."
As part of the Aviator beta process, Harrison put the hub's orchestrator agent, Avi, to work on real, day-to-day compliance questions. Work that traditionally meant combing through transaction grids line-by-line was surfaced for review in a fraction of the time, with Harrison retaining full control over which findings to act on.
Primark
Primark has partnered with Kallikor to introduce a simulation led approach to supply chain decisions. The aim being for the retailer to test and validate operational and capital changes before implementation.
The tie up begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing teams to test alternative operating configurations before implementation.
By comparing scenarios in a simulated environment, the retailer says it can identify more efficient approaches while protecting customer service and avoiding downstream cost or operational impacts across the store estate.
Adam Hoccom, Director of Supply Chain at Primark, says: “As we continue to grow across markets, ensuring our supply chain is designed to support that ambition is critical."
"A key part of that is making sure our distribution centres operate efficiently while remaining aligned to store needs. Working with Kallikor allows us to test and compare different operating configurations - from layout and flow changes within sites to broader network considerations - before we commit capital spend."
"This gives us greater confidence in the choices we make and how they will perform in practice, strengthening our ability to innovate and make well informed decisions as we evolve our network.”
Walmart and Wing
Starting on 21st October, Walmart customers in Charlotte, USA can order drone delivery powered by Wing. This marks the official launch of this service in the region.
Over the next year, Wing and Walmart are expanding drone delivery to 270+ stores, with a view to building a coast to coast network in 2027, ultimately reaching over 10% of the US population.
Bypassing heavy traffic, inclement weather and crowded parking lots, residents can get game day supplies, routine essentials, and weeknight dinners delivered straight to their yard.
Ikea
Ikea UK is investing £31.5 million across its Peterborough and Doncaster customer distribution centres (CDC) as the retailer aims to make online fulfilment more efficient and sustainable. In Peterborough, new technology is packaging customer orders to size and reducing material usage by up to 30%, by preventing waste from oversized boxes and filling paper. In Doncaster, Ikea is trialling a new regional fulfilment capability, serving customers in the north and Scotland from a closer location to them.
The investments will strengthen Ikea’s UK fulfilment network as online sales account for 43.3% of total UK sales in financial year 2026. It is investing £30 million in new technology for its Peterborough CDC, with the upgrades taking place over a two-year period. As part of this, it has launched new PackSize technology to prevent waste from oversized cardboard boxes and filling materials by packaging customer orders to size. On average, the technology reduces material usage by up to 30% and void fill by up to 60%.
The technology is expected to increase the share of parcels processed through automation at the Peterborough CDC from 47% today to 75% in 2027, helping the fulfilment team prepare orders for delivery more efficiently. These additional orders would otherwise have been packaged by manually creating a packing carton which includes having to measure the article then creating the cartons to fit the order. Three drones and nests were introduced at the site in January to support inventory management. They scan each aisle in short cycles, helping Ikea to keep stock in the right place and meet customer demand.
Ikea is investing £1.5 million in trialling a new fulfilment capability at its Doncaster CDC. The site now fulfils orders for customers in the Gateshead, Edinburgh and Glasgow areas, with plans for Sheffield to follow. By fulfilling these orders from Doncaster rather than Peterborough, Ikea expects to reduce emissions from delivery journeys by an estimated 280 tonnes of CO2 annually. The new capability has created an additional 80 jobs at the Doncaster site.
Co-op
The number of retail crime cases solved has almost doubled during a new crime reporting trial between Co-op and Devon and Cornwall Police in the UK. The partnership, according to those involved, delivers significantly faster justice for offences carried out, with data from Devon & Cornwall Police showing crimes reported through the platform - which is called SentrySIS - achieving a solve rate of almost 60%, which is approaching double the force’s average solve rate for retail crime versus retail crime being reported by those using traditional channels.
Data from Devon & Cornwall Police also revealed that 90% of identified shop theft offenders are repeat offenders, with just 50 individuals responsible for around a quarter of all shop theft offences in the Devon and Cornwall force area, often with more than 100 known offences each. The new system enables stronger intelligence sharing; improved tracking of repeat offenders - connecting multiple offences committed by the same individual and building stronger cases against prolific offenders and, closer collaboration with police both at a local and central level.
Store colleagues upload incident details, CCTV, photos and impact statement enabling police to record and allocate the crime in as little 30 minutes - a process that could take police up to seven days. Furthermore, it removes the need for investigating officers to then approach the retailer for evidence, saving time for retailers and resulting in the average time taken for investigations to be completed and assigned an outcome being slashed by more than a third to 35 days.
The success of the pilot has seen the SentrySIS system, which links to Co-op’s wider partnership working with UK Partners Against Crime (UKPAC), now activated across all Co-op stores in Devon and Cornwall, with discussions now underway with additional police forces. Co-op’s own retail crime levels are falling with the retailer expected to see its lowest levels since the pandemic.
Brompton
Commerce reports that Brompton, a British foldable bicycle manufacturer, has launched its new partner portal on BigCommerce B2B Edition.
The aim here is to give Brompton’s global network of independent retailers a modern ordering experience, with the portal running on the same BigCommerce instance and product catalogue that powers the company’s direct-to-consumer business.
Brompton first launched its composable direct-to-consumer site on BigCommerce in 2024. The new offering extends that foundation to the wholesale side of the business, which accounts for roughly 75% of Brompton’s total sales across over 1,000 retail partners worldwide.
“Our retail partners are central to Brompton's success. The new Partner Portal gives them a modern, intuitive way to explore our product range, place orders and access the information they need to support our joint customers.” says Oliver Boardman, CTO at Brompton. “This investment is about making it easier for our partners to do business with Brompton and grow alongside us.”
Five Below
poq has announced the launch of new native iOS and Android mobile apps for Five Below. Tiffany D’Amato, Vice President of Digital, Five Below, comments: “Our customers live on their phones, and these apps give them a faster, more engaging way to experience everything they love about Five Below.”
“Partnering with poq allowed us to bring that vision to life quickly and effectively, with a truly native experience built for our shoppers. We’re confident these apps will drive stronger customer engagement and long-term growth for the brand.”
Helen Slaven, Chief Revenue Officer at poq, says: “Five Below is exactly the kind of brand app commerce was made for, with a huge, engaged customer base and a shopping experience built on discovery. We are thrilled to partner with them to turn mobile into an owned channel that retains customers, grows lifetime value and scales with the business.”
A built-in price scanner lets shoppers scan an item in store and check its price and details on the spot, while personalised search helps customers explore the various products Five Below has to offer. Store aware features surface the nearest store and stock availability and push notifications, keep customers close to new arrivals and seasonal drops. The apps are built on poq’s platform and integrated with the Five Below commercetools commerce stack.
SPAR International
Footprints AI and SPAR International have announced a partnership to develop a media marketplace that supports independently operated food retail. The platform would be available to all SPAR licensees, enabling SPAR country organisations to access a single platform to plan, buy, optimise, and measure retail media campaigns, with the same simplicity, precision, and sales tracking as digital advertising.
Footprints AI’s software sits on top of SPAR country organisations’ existing physical and digital retail infrastructure (stores, screens, instore radio, e-commerce, mobile apps, and PoS data) and connects it into one advertiser facing marketplace, while ensuring each organisation keeps full control of its own data, assets, and commercial model.
“Retail media has reached a point where brands and agencies no longer need an isolated network. They need a marketplace that can scale outcomes. The first phase of retail media was about individual retailers monetising their own assets. The next phase is global marketplace infrastructure: advertisers get a more consistent way to plan, buy, optimise, and measure retail media across markets, while local retailers keep control of their data, assets, and commercial model. That is the shift we are building with SPAR,” says Dan Marc, CEO, Footprints AI.
“Retail media is an important growth platform in modern retail. At SPAR our ambition is to connect the strength of our global SPAR network with the power of local retail entrepreneurship, creating a scalable platform that delivers value for customers, retailers and brand partners alike."
"By combining our vast physical presence, shopper relationships and data capabilities with advanced retail media technology, we are evolving our SPAR network into a connected commercial ecosystem that enables brands to engage consumers more effectively across markets while generating new revenue opportunities for SPAR country organisations,” says Tobias Wasmuht, CEO, SPAR International.
AliExpress
AliExpress has announced a partnership that brings its global product selection into YouTube’s creator ecosystem, giving eligible creators access to various products to feature in their content, along with new commission earning opportunities.
Following the launch of the collaboration in South Korea in March, the partnership will expand to four markets: the United States, Brazil, the United Kingdom and Germany. Further expansion will take place in phases, in line with the roll-out of YouTube’s affiliate programme in new markets.
With YouTube's recent extension of its Shopping Affiliate Programme to eligible creators in Germany and the United Kingdom, the partnership will connect participating creators not only in Europe but also eventually worldwide with AliExpress's product offerings. A particular focus is Brand+ - a dedicated selection of branded products from international and local brands.
Creators can discover and select AliExpress products directly within YouTube Studio. The integration connects AliExpress products with YouTube's three major content formats - long-form videos, shorts, and livestreams - allowing creators to tag shoppable product recommendations across key moments of audience discovery and engagement.
They can explore AliExpress's products across categories such as consumer electronics, sports and outdoor, home and living, and lifestyle. Using data on bestselling and trending products, they can handpick items that resonate with their audiences. Viewers can link directly from YouTube to AliExpress to complete their purchases.
Matalan
Matalan reports that its first fully native app has recorded 1.76 million downloads since launching in August, with monthly active users growing by 10% month-on-month since go live. App orders increased 20% year-on-year in August and 28% in September, while conversion has reached 4.4%, ahead of its 3.4% target. Average order value is also 14% higher than on Matalan's website.
Developed in partnership with Apadmi, features include intelligent search to help customers find products more easily, richer product content and streamlined checkout through Apple Pay and Google Pay.
The app also brings Matalan Me rewards and account information together in one place, making it easier for customers to access their benefits and personalised offers.
It is designed to connect Matalan's digital and physical shopping experiences. An in-store barcode scanning feature allows customers to check product details, availability and reviews using their phones, helping them move more easily between shopping in-store and online.
Samsung Electronics
Samsung Electronics and Checkout.com have announced a global partnership across Samsung’s digital commerce ecosystem. Samsung Electronics has 221 operational sites across 76 countries. Its broad portfolio spans mobile devices, consumer electronics, software, connected experiences and digital commerce, including Samsung.com, Galaxy Store, Samsung Wallet and Samsung Pay.
Checkout.com currently processes payments for Samsung Gulf Electronics, supporting Samsung.com across the MENA region. Under the aforementioned partnership, Checkout.com will extend its support to additional Samsung Electronics’ digital commerce environments and markets in the EU and North America across both the Galaxy Store and Samsung.com.
The partnership will bring together Checkout.com’s global and local acquiring capabilities, payment processing platform and payment optimisation technology to support Samsung Electronics’ payment flows as it expands across markets. Samsung Electronics will use its Intelligent Acceptance, an AI powered solution that uses real-time data from Checkout.com’s global network to help optimise transactions, reduce payment failures and improve performance.
Samsung Pay will also launch on Flow, Checkout.com's low code payments integration, on 31st October. This gives Checkout.com merchants a new way to add Samsung Pay as a digital wallet option for online and in-app checkout and tap into over one billion Samsung Galaxy phone users.
Debenhams Group
Debenhams Group, which is home to Debenhams, Karen Millen, boohoo, MAN and PrettyLittleThing, has launched a new cash flow solution with the aim of giving its 30,000+ brand partners faster access to sales revenue as soon as orders are shipped.
Now live on Debenhams ahead of the Christmas trading period, Storfund’s Daily Advance solution allows partners to access their sales revenue daily, rather than waiting for the standard marketplace payment cycle.
Dan Finley, CEO at Debenhams Group, says: “Our marketplace-led strategy is built on creating an ecosystem where great brands can scale with us. As we grow our marketplaces, we want to make Debenhams Group the partner of choice for brands looking to reach millions of customers and accelerate their growth. Giving sellers faster access to their sales revenue gives them greater flexibility to reinvest in their businesses when they need it most - particularly as we head into peak Christmas trading. It’s another example of how we’re supporting our 30,000+ brands and making it easier to do business with Debenhams Group.”
Justin Hanna, Director of Platform Partnerships at Storfund, says: “Marketplaces have spent the last decade building better shopping, advertising, fulfilment and settlement experiences. Liquidity is the next frontier. When businesses have cash on hand to respond to demand, buy stock and invest in growth, that benefits the entire marketplace. Embedding Daily Advance within Debenhams gives sellers greater control over their cash flow at a crucial point in their growth.”
Klarna and Fiserv
Klarna has announced its availability on Commerce Hub, Fiserv's enterprise commerce platform, for the first time. Merchants in the US, Canada, the UK and select European markets will be able to offer Klarna both in-store and online.
The agreement follows the buy now pay later specialist’s launch this week at 100,000 US in-store merchant locations through Clover, Fiserv's PoS platform for small businesses.
"We're rapidly expanding Klarna's footprint in physical retail, now live in 100,000 physical locations across the US through Clover," says David Sykes, Chief Commercial Officer at Klarna. "Deepening our integration with Fiserv's Commerce Hub allows us to support merchants across channels. We're giving consumers clear, flexible ways to pay, with a new credit decision made on every transaction."
“Consumers expect flexibility wherever they shop, and merchants need technology that enables consistent experiences across every channel," says Sanjay Saraf, Chief Product Officer, Merchant Solutions, Fiserv.
"By expanding our partnership with Klarna through Clover and Commerce Hub, we're helping businesses offer more payment choice, connect their in-store and digital experiences, drive growth and customer loyalty.”
Muffato Group
Sensei has deployed its technology in a new Muffato Go store in Curitiba, Brazil. This has been developed in partnership with supermarket specialist Grupo Muffato.
While Sensei first became known for its autonomous store technology, it says that the intelligence behind those stores has always been designed to address a broader challenge: giving physical retail the ability and the data to understand and automate its own operations in real-time.
The new Muffato Go, according to those involved, will put that capability into practice, showing how the same underlying technology can improve shelf availability, detect losses, automate checkout, manage fresh products and support online order fulfillment.
Headquartered in Portugal and operating across Europe and Brazil, Sensei has deployed its technology in more than 100 autonomous points of sale, including the world's largest autonomous store, opened in Leiria, Portugal, in 2025.
“The new Muffato Go shows what AI can already do in a physical store. Shoppers get a faster, simpler way to buy, but that is only the visible part. Our models recognise products and shopper interactions as they happen, and store teams get the right task at the right time," says Vasco Portugal, CEO and Co-founder at Sensei.
"The real value is turning what happens in the store into intelligence that supports the entire business, from the shop floor to the head office. That is what we mean by Conscious Spaces: physical spaces that see, understand and act."
Old Spike
Old Spike, a specialty coffee roaster and social enterprise, has opened its seventh London café in Southwark.
The new Great Suffolk Street location displays what it believes to be the UK hospitality industry’s first live impact dashboard powered by payments platform, Square.
Old Spike’s central mission is to create employment for people experiencing homelessness. Its Barista Training and Employment Programme provides practical training, paid work placements and support into lasting work. Since opening in 2015, over 350 people have completed its training course.
The dashboard uses Square data to display to customers how their purchases across Old Spike’s seven cafés contribute to its training and paid work placement programme. Southwark is the first café to feature the dashboard, which Old Spike plans to roll-out across all its sites.
When a purchase is made, Square automatically sends the information to the Impact Dashboard system, which records the transaction and calculates the relevant impact measures and KPIs. These figures are turned into visuals via an animation application so they can be displayed on public-facing screens. The dashboard showcases the number of trainees completing the programme, graduates securing lasting employment and the amount paid during work placements.
The canimations for the dashboard screens were created by motion and data visualisation studio Algo which developed a modular animation system powered by Rive, the same technology behind Spotify’s Wrapped campaign.
Booker Wholesale
Booker Wholesale has deployed more than 500 Sony BRAVIA Professional Displays to establish a new retail media network across 100 of its UK locations. The project was delivered by Pixel Inspiration in partnership with dunnhumby.
Installed predominantly at rack ends and above palletised merchandise, the displays provide a platform for targeted advertising and promotional content, while integrating into the existing wholesale environment. This presented specific challenges for the installation.
Displays needed to be positioned for maximum visibility while also being protected against accidental impacts from stock movement, pallet handling and day-to-day warehouse operations.
Sony BZ35L BRAVIA Professional Displays were selected as part of the hardware solution to provide the combination of image quality, reliability and operational efficiency required for the network.
To provide additional protection, Pixel Inspiration worked with UNICOL to develop a combined mounting and protective shroud solution. This was designed to withstand the demands of a busy cash and carry environment while maintaining appropriate airflow and ventilation around the displays.
The displays use Sony’s Android-based System on Chip (SoC) technology, reducing the need for additional external media players and helping simplify the overall installation. The network is managed through the DISE content management system, enabling campaign content to be centrally targeted and distributed across Booker’s national estate.

items.title: How retail delivery fleets can cut turbo downtime and waste
items.summary: Retailers have spent years refining websites, apps and warehouse systems to promise faster delivery, yet the final link in that chain is still a van travelling down a residential street, relying on mechanical components that wear out.For retailers running their own home delivery operations or contra
items.body:
Retailers have spent years refining websites, apps and warehouse systems to promise faster delivery, yet the final link in that chain is still a van travelling down a residential street, relying on mechanical components that wear out.
For retailers running their own home delivery operations or contracting last mile partners, fleet reliability has a direct bearing on customer satisfaction.
How Much Pressure Is on Delivery Vans?
Van use across Great Britain remains at historically high levels. The Department for Transport's road traffic estimates show that vans covered 58.8 billion vehicle miles in 2025, broadly level with 2024 and 10.0% higher than in 2019. That growth has coincided with the expansion of online shopping and home delivery.
Electrification is progressing, but more slowly in the commercial sector than many forecasts suggested. Figures from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders show that battery electric vans made up 2.2% of the vans in service on UK roads in 2025. For the foreseeable future, most delivery fleets will continue to run turbocharged diesel engines, which makes turbo health a current operational concern rather than a legacy issue.
Why Do Delivery Routes Wear Turbos Faster?
Last-mile work is unusually tough on forced induction. A typical route involves dozens of stops, frequent restarts, long idling periods at loading bays and short hops that never allow the engine to reach full operating temperature. These conditions encourage oil degradation and soot build-up, both of which shorten turbo life. Diesel particulate filters that cannot regenerate properly on low-speed routes raise exhaust back pressure and add further strain.
When a turbo fails on a delivery van, the cost spreads across the operation. Parcels must be redistributed, delivery slots are missed and drivers may be left without a van for their shift. Across a large fleet, a handful of unplanned failures each month can undermine service-level agreements and customer ratings.
How Can Telematics Help Predict Failures?
Telematics platforms can read engine fault codes in real time, flag deviations in boost pressure and track changes in fuel consumption that may point to an underperforming turbo. Some systems also monitor oil service intervals and driver behaviour, such as harsh acceleration or shutting the engine down immediately after heavy running.
Linking that data to the maintenance schedule allows workshops to inspect a van before a small fault becomes a roadside breakdown. Patterns across the fleet can also reveal whether failures cluster on particular routes, models or depots, which helps managers address root causes rather than individual symptoms.
Should Fleets Buy New or Exchange?
At fleet level, the choice of replacement part becomes a procurement decision with operational and financial consequences.
A new turbo suits vans still under warranty, cases where provenance matters for leasing or resale, and situations where the original part has been badly damaged. It offers fresh components throughout, but it carries the highest unit cost and may involve longer lead times on less common models.
An exchange programme works differently. The workshop fits a ready-built unit from stock and the failed turbo is returned as a core, which can then be remanufactured and put back into circulation. For fleets, a reliable exchange arrangement keeps vans on the road with minimal downtime while smoothing costs across a large number of repairs. Agreeing stock levels in advance with turbo suppliers for the turbo types most common in the fleet makes the process quicker still.
Where Does Sustainability Reporting Come In?
Retailers face growing expectations to report on the environmental impact of their operations, including the emissions and resources linked to logistics. Turbo choice is a small but measurable part of that picture.
Remanufacturing and reconditioning reuse the housings and other durable components of a failed unit rather than sending them for scrap, which reduces demand for newly manufactured parts. Recording the number of exchanged and remanufactured components alongside fuel and emissions data gives fleet teams a straightforward way to evidence circular practices within wider sustainability reports.
How Should Fleet Teams Plan Maintenance?
A structured approach combines several elements. Service schedules work best when they reflect real duty cycles rather than generic mileage intervals, with shorter oil change periods for vans on intensive urban routes. Telematics alerts are most useful when they feed directly into workshop booking systems. Spare turbo availability, whether through a stocked turbo exchange programme or supplier agreements, can be planned around the models that make up most of the fleet. Failed units are also worth analysing to identify underlying causes such as oil contamination or blocked filters.
For retailers competing on delivery speed, a well maintained van is part of the customer experience. Treating turbo health as a planned, data-led activity rather than an emergency repair protects both service levels and operating margins.

items.title: I turned 40 and booked the Silk Road trip of my childhood dreams

items.body:
I turned 40 and booked the Silk Road trip of my childhood dreams
Uzbekistan is a pinnacle of the Silk Road but remains fairly undiscovered. Hannah Copeland went in search of childhood fantasies and got lost in vibrant bazaars
My fascination with Central Asia began as a teenager when I read a historical romance novel about an Uzbek Princess and her travels along the Silk Road. The epic landscapes and sense of adventure made it a bucket list destination for me. Two decades later, I was finally making it a reality.
Just getting to Uzbekistan is an experience, starting with the cultural jolt that is Uzbekistan Airways, which left me wondering if I’d boarded a plane to a parallel universe. Most of my fellow passengers appeared to be Uzbeks returning home with designer hauls from Istanbul airport, many of the women flashing their distinctive capped gold teeth (historically a symbol of status and beauty), and the men wearing traditional square ‘doppa’ hats. Others were decked out in Kazakh and Mongolian embroidered robes, leaving me well and truly the sore thumb as I headed to Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan.
Like many sprawling Central Asian cities, Tashkent still has remnants of Eastern bloc influence, with concrete, brutalist architecture that couldn’t be described as beautiful, exactly, but is impressive nonetheless. A shallow earthquake right under the city in 1966 destroyed much of the historic centre, with Soviet planners rebuilding it to showcase state power.
The Silk Road in style
It’s a fascinating mix of old and new: imposing statues of bygone conquerors stand alongside mosques with intricate mosaic domes, wide boulevards and leafy parks, bustling bazaars, modern restaurants, and contemporary skyscrapers. Ancient Islamic history and grand artistic design clashes with a youthful vibe from the influx of students and young professionals.
I was on a seven-day tour operated by Cox & Kings. Established in 1758, it is the world’s oldest travel company, and its tours include access to incredible on-the-ground experts and experiences. Mine included hotels, as well as local food and drink.
Tashkent’s Old City is a dense maze of traditional clay houses and narrow lanes. I took the metro from the hotel, not because cars weren’t available, but because in Tashkent, public transport is high culture. Uzbek architects and Soviet authorities designed stations as ‘palaces of the people’, the system doubling as an underground art gallery, with marble-clad walls, murals of cosmonauts, and glass chandeliers hanging from the rafters.
With blue mosaic domes, intricately carved Indian sandalwood doors and gold interiors, the Tillya Sheikh mosque is the city’s most commanding attraction. It’s also home to one of the world’s oldest Qur’ans, written in the 7th century. During my visit there was only a smattering of tourists, and some groups of local children flying colourful kites as part of the Eid celebrations.
Everyday Uzbek life
In the weeks before I arrived, 20,000 people gathered each morning to pray in the square. Most locals are curious, open, and fiercely proud of their heritage. In the nearby Abu Bakr Kaffal Shashi Mausoleum, a praying family told me the story of the Imam buried there, who was their great-great (many times over) grandfather.
In contrast to the serenity of the square, Chorsu Bazaar introduced me to everyday Uzbek life. It is a vibrant spectacle that wallops the senses. One of the most iconic markets in Central Asia, traders have for centuries sold everything from silk Ikat kimonos to hearty local delicacies like plov (a fragrant and oily medley of rice, veg, meat and spices).
I have to admit some of the bubbling pots and food displays were more alien than haute cuisine, but the smorgasbord of dishes I tried – including dill salad, quails eggs, pickles, mutton pie and lemon tea – was thankfully devoid of some of the slimier offerings I spotted (most notably Hisab, a huge sausage with intestinal casing resembling some sort of monster eel.) Pomegranate juice made fresh with a curious contraption, like an oversized lemon-squeezer, was both bitter and delicious.
Madrasahs, mosques and minarets
The ancient city of Bukhara, an hour-and-a-half’s internal flight away, took me deeper into this landlocked country. On the edge of the vast Kyzylkum Desert, it is one of the most complete examples of a medieval Islamic city. Like Tashkent, it has an urbanised part and a contrasting Old Town, where intriguing architectural attractions include madrasahs, mosques and minarets.
These are relics of a time when the city was one of the main destinations on the Silk Road, when merchants travelled across the globe connecting East and West, exchanging goods, culture and ideas between Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
What struck me most was how I saw traces of Western European, Turkish, Persian, Central Asian, Russian and Chinese influence woven in the food, clothing and language.
As a hoarder of cultural treasures, I was in heaven browsing stalls touting handmade carpets, silk embroidery (suzani), miniature paintings and ceramics. Every beautiful thing I bought came from small family businesses, and was a way to engage with local artists and learn about traditions passed through generations.
Cox & Kings take guests off the traditional tourist routes, and one curiosity in Bukhara was an opulent, bizarre tearoom called the Retro Saloon Timur. The venue is hidden down a winding back street so tucked away it would evade even the most inquisitive tourist. It serves teas and homemade jams, but what stays with you are the surroundings: every centimetre of wall space is covered by a mix of paintings, from desert scenes to tasteful nudes and grand military portraiture.
High speed Afrosiyob train
Gaudy golden ornaments adorn every other orifice: mannequins in elaborate historical costumes grace corners and a mix of Russian and Central Asian music provides a backdrop to AI-generated princes and princesses on TV screens. I’m not quite sure whether owner Irina Sharipova’s intention was ironic tackiness or serious cultural commentary, but either way, it was huge fun: charming and memorable.
A particularly special evening was spent on the rooftop of Minorai Kalon Boutique Hotel, where I dined al fresco on lamb stew and rosemary potatoes, a mixture of local salads, dill sour cream and pickles, homemade bread and soups. The restaurant overlooks a skyline dominated by a moonlit Po-i-Kalyan mosque and minaret as the call to prayer rings out across the city.
The next day, I took the high-speed Afrosiyob train to Samarkand, the ultimate destination on any Uzbek itinerary and a city that has held profound wonder for me since those geeky childhood bookworm days, owing to its mystique and Silk Road history.
The train service was clean, efficient, and modern. You even get a snack of ice cream with raspberries included with the ticket. Over the two-hour journey, I listened to a playlist of Central Asian music while watching the Uzbek countryside zoom past, imagining how caravans of traders once made this expedition on foot or camel.
Pre-cursor to the Taj Mahal
One of the oldest cities in the world, celebrated for its unparalleled beauty and historical significance, Samarkand has been a cultural crossroads for thousands of years. This is largely due to geography: its fertile, water-rich location was the junction where Central Asia’s impassable mountains and harsh deserts forced trade routes from China, India, and Persia to converge.
The central Registan Square holds a trio of madrasahs, or historic Islamic places of study, with the Ulugh Beg, Sher-Dor, and Tilya-Kori each boasting wonderful decorative mosaic frontages. Just a short walk from the Registan is the Bibi-Khanym Mosque, considered by many to be a precursor to the Taj Mahal, which was built some 200 years later (Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur commissioned the building for his wife in the 15th century).
Before I left, I asked our guide Bobur if he could take me to morning prayer at a small mosque near our hotel. It was worth the early rise to see the city at dawn, hear the Imam chant and witness men, young and old, at their daily ritual of worship in the shadow of the minaret. When they noticed me watching they gestured to the women’s section of the temple, a simple but beautiful room with a rug to pray on, where chinks of morning light seep through a carved wooden door and make an intricate pattern beside the Qur’an. I found it profoundly moving and felt a strong connection to the quiet and welcoming spirit of the place.
There are few places on earth that feed my childlike imagination and conjure such excitement as Central Asia. I have never been anywhere with such a fusion of ancient cultures and landscapes. The trip whetted my appetite not only to explore the region more fully, but to delve deeper into the country, a destination many avoid in favour of tickbox express tours that can’t possibly do the ‘Stans’ justice. Uzbekistan is both enduring and alive – I’m so grateful to have explored before mass tourism arrives.
How to travel the Silk Road
Cox & Kings (coxandkingstravel.com) offers a 12 day small group tour, Uzbekistan: Heart of Central Asia, from £3,895pp, based on two sharing. Price includes international and internal flights, high-speed rail and all transfers, accommodation, guided sightseeing, entrance fees and select meals.

items.title: Oxford Street goes traffic-free as Sadiq Khan launches pedestrianisation
items.summary: Oxford Street has become permanently traffic-free for the first time as London mayor Sadiq Khan presses ahead with a major overhaul of the capital’s busiest shopping district ahead of Christmas. Almost a kilometre of the famous shopping street, between Orchard Street near Selfridges and Great Portland Street, has closed to vehicles from Monday, ending decades [...]
items.body:
Oxford Street goes traffic-free as Sadiq Khan launches pedestrianisation
Oxford Street has become permanently traffic-free for the first time as London mayor Sadiq Khan presses ahead with a major overhaul of the capital’s busiest shopping district ahead of Christmas.
Almost a kilometre of the famous shopping street, between Orchard Street near Selfridges and Great Portland Street, has closed to vehicles from Monday, ending decades of failed attempts to pedestrianise the West End thoroughfare.
Buses, taxis, private hire vehicles, cyclists and scooters will now be diverted onto surrounding roads, while deliveries will be restricted to overnight hours between midnight and 7am.
The move marks the first phase of a wider regeneration project aimed at reviving Oxford Street, which generates around £3.1bn in annual spending but has struggled with changing shopping habits, empty storefronts and the proliferation of American-style sweet shops.
Khan described the closure as a “truly momentous occasion for the capital”, arguing that removing traffic would help attract investment, retailers and visitors back to the West End.
“There has been talk of pedestrianising Oxford Street for decades. After so many false dawns, and now working with a Government who share the scale of my ambition, I’m proud that we’re finally unlocking a new era for the street”, he said.
The mayor has also suggested the transformation could help replace the low-quality souvenir and sweet shops that have become increasingly prominent along the street.
“I’m looking forward to good quality shops rather than the dross we’ve had”, he told the Evening Standard.
Retailers back plans as traffic concerns remain
The pedestrianisation comes just weeks before the crucial Christmas trading period, with major retailers welcoming the prospect of increased footfall.
John Lewis, which has traded on Oxford Street for more than 160 years, said the changes would complement its multimillion-pound investment in its flagship store.
Selfridges also backed the plans, while property adviser Savills reported growing competition among retailers seeking space on the street.
“We’re experiencing unprecedented appetite from brands for space on Oxford Street, with competition for prime units continuing to intensify,” said Sam Foyle, Savills’ co-head of global retail.
However, the scheme has faced opposition from residents and Westminster City Council over concerns that diverting traffic will increase congestion on neighbouring roads.
Buses and other vehicles will be redirected through surrounding streets, including Wigmore Street, Henrietta Place and Cavendish Place, with new bus stops approximately 200 metres from the pedestrianised area.
Westminster Council deputy leader Tim Barnes has criticised the timetable, arguing that the scheme has been rushed.
“It feels rushed, it feels under-resourced, and it feels slightly undercooked,” he said.
Transport for London said it would closely monitor traffic movements and make adjustments where necessary.
London’s Transport Commissioner Andy Lord said the authority would be “closely monitoring these changes to make sure they are working for everyone”.
The closure follows years of political disagreement between City Hall and Westminster Council, which blocked an earlier pedestrianisation proposal in 2018.
Khan eventually established the Oxford Street Development Corporation, transferring key planning powers away from the council to a mayoral body overseeing the regeneration.
The move has drawn criticism from local residents who argue that it reduces their influence over decisions affecting surrounding neighbourhoods.
For now, the street will operate under temporary arrangements designed to minimise disruption during the Christmas shopping season.
More substantial improvements are scheduled for spring 2027, including more than 50 trees, over 100 seats, two public squares, dining areas and new lighting.
The Mayor hopes the redevelopment will help Oxford Street compete with major international shopping destinations including the Champs-Élysées in Paris and La Rambla in Barcelona

items.body:
Sadiq Khan has been trying to pedestrianise Oxford Street since he first became the mayor of London in 2016. On Monday, after numerous setbacks, his plan will finally come to fruition. The busiest stretch of the nation’s famous shopping street will be closed to traffic in a scheme designed to improve the area and make it more attractive to pedestrians. It should be an emblematic case study in making cities greener, less congested, more inviting places to live and visit.
The Greater London Authority hopes it will rejuvenate a high street fallen on hard times. Since the pandemic, the number of vacant shops on Oxford Street has more than quadrupled. It estimates that the scheme will generate £82m of value a year in the area by increasing footfall and encouraging visitors to linger. This impact remains to be seen, but research from other cities suggests that shops experience higher sales once an area is pedestrianised. Given the prime minister’s focus on rejuvenating British high streets, whose dilapidation is correlated with support for Reform UK, he should be watching with interest.
The benefits of pedestrianisation are far greater than increased shopping. Domestic transport remains the largest contributor to greenhouse-gas emissions in Britain. This sector’s emissions have fallen more slowly than others largely because too many people still rely on cars. Mr Khan’s city is an outlier: 59% of all journeys in Britain were made by car in 2024, while in London cars accounted for 34%. This is hardly surprising when the Treasury spends twice as much on London’s transport system as it does on other regions in England, and the capital’s bus fares are cheaper. In Leeds, which has no mass-transit system, nearly half of people drive to work. Car use cannot be reduced without simultaneously improving public transport.
The critics of pedestrianisation – including Westminster council – suggest it merely displaces traffic elsewhere. But the evidence on this is more nuanced. One study from the University of the West of England suggests the closure of strategic roads causes some traffic to disappear permanently, as people switch to public transport or walk. Low-traffic neighbourhoods (LTNs), the pedestrianisation schemes that were rushed through in the capital during Covid-19 and have since been introduced in Manchester and Birmingham, were fiercely criticised for causing a buildup of road traffic elsewhere. Yet one study of 46 LTNs in London suggested their impact on traffic elsewhere was minimal.
Car-free areas should be accompanied by other policies that reduce pollution on surrounding roads, such as the low-emissions zones introduced in London and Oxford. Mr Khan was criticised by the then leader of the opposition, Keir Starmer, for the expansion of Ulez in 2023, and also suffered racial abuse. He has since been vindicated by research from Imperial College suggesting Ulez has significantly improved the health of primary school children in the capital, whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution.
That Transport for London estimates the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will have only a minimal impact on nitrogen dioxide emissions, which were already decreasing as a result of Ulez, is testimony to the policy’s success. In 2014, Oxford Street had the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. Its pedestrianisation should be an inspiration to other cities to embrace policies that work for people, not cars.

items.title: Immersive physical activations and AI powered experiences: last week's most read retail technology articles
items.summary: Check out our most clicked retail technology articles from last week, including Azoma, Westfield Rise, Lionsgate, Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Foot Locker, Stylitics, Co-op, Five Below, poq, Firstwork, and the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.Agentic commerce platform Azoma raises $11.2 million
items.body:
Check out our most clicked retail technology articles from last week, including Azoma, Westfield Rise, Lionsgate, Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Foot Locker, Stylitics, Co-op, Five Below, poq, Firstwork, and the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
Agentic commerce platform Azoma raises $11.2 million in Series A round led by Puma Growth Partners
AI shopping agents startup, Azoma, has announced a $11.2 million Series A funding round led by Puma Growth Partners, with participation from dunnhumby, Twin Path, MaRS IAF, Rank Ventures and Ignite Ventures and Angels from Google DeepMind and Legora.
The round will fund the expansion of Azoma's platform across the AI personal assistants space such as ChatGPT Dots and Meta Muse; as well as the build out of its optimisation and attribution capabilities for enterprise consumer brands utilising dunnhumby data.
The cash will also support team growth with a particular focus on recruiting AI talent. Azoma works with consumer brands including L'Oréal, Unilever, Mars, Beiersdorf and Reckitt. The round follows a $4 million seed announced in December 2025.
Azoma was founded in 2022 by Max Sinclair, a former Amazon executive; and Timur Luguev, a PhD and Postdoctoral Researcher in machine learning. Sinclair comments: "Three hundred and fifty million people used Alexa for Shopping last year. Walmart customers who use their AI shopping assistant Sparky spend 40% more than those who don’t."
"Instinct, the personal AI Assistant that launched in August with zero marketing budget, already accounts for $1 billion in transactions, and is growing at a rate of 10% day over day. Agent-to-agent commerce has arrived faster than anyone expected. For our customers, this will be more transformational than the internet. Agentic commerce will be on a par with how electrification birthed or transformed these enterprise consumer brands."
John Lewis, Asda, Morrisons, H&M, Dunelm, and Waitrose among 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards finalists
We're hugely pleased to present the finalists and shortlists for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards, sponsored by 3D Cloud, Business France, and Retail Technology Show 2027. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Westfield Rise and Lionsgate launch Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping immersive experience in London
Westfield Rise, the in-house retail media agency of Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW), has partnered with Lionsgate to launch The Hunger Games: The Capitol Experience, an exclusive immersive activation at Westfield London. Running from 30th October to 23rd November, the free ticketed experience will give fans the chance to step into the world of Panem ahead of the release of the movie.
Located in The Atrium at Westfield London, it will feature a Cornucopia installation, interactive moments inspired by the film, exclusive collectibles and a world exclusive film clip available only to visitors attending the activation. The activation forms part of Lionsgate’s wider campaign for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which the studio has described as its largest above the line campaign of 2026, spanning TV, VOD, outdoor, social, digital, radio, PR, influencer and brand partnership activity.
Westfield will support the campaign through its owned marketing channels, including social media, CRM, digital platforms, editorial content, in-centre media and ticketing communications. The partnership also extends across URW's Northern European portfolio.
Supporting activity at Westfield Täby Centrum and Westfield Mall of the Netherlands will help amplify the campaign through local marketing, social content and customer communications. Additional campaign activity will also take place at Westfield Chodov in Prague.
Co-op and Devon & Cornwall Police double retail crime cases solves with new reporting system roll-out
The partnership, according to those involved, delivers significantly faster justice for offences carried out, with data from Devon & Cornwall Police showing crimes reported through the platform - which is called SentrySIS - achieving a solve rate of almost 60%, which is approaching double the force’s average solve rate for retail crime versus retail crime being reported by those using traditional channels.
Data from Devon & Cornwall Police also revealed that 90% of identified shop theft offenders are repeat offenders, with just 50 individuals responsible for around a quarter of all shop theft offences in the Devon and Cornwall force area, often with more than 100 known offences each.
The new system enables stronger intelligence sharing; improved tracking of repeat offenders - connecting multiple offences committed by the same individual and building stronger cases against prolific offenders and, closer collaboration with police both at a local and central level.
Store colleagues upload incident details, CCTV, photos and impact statement enabling police to record and allocate the crime in as little 30 minutes - a process that could take police up to seven days.
Furthermore, it removes the need for investigating officers to then approach the retailer for evidence, saving time for retailers and resulting in the average time taken for investigations to be completed and assigned an outcome being slashed by more than a third to 35 days.
The success of the pilot has seen the SentrySIS system, which links to Co-op’s wider partnership working with UK Partners Against Crime (UKPAC), now activated across all Co-op stores in Devon and Cornwall, with discussions now underway with additional police forces. Co-op’s own retail crime levels are falling with the retailer expected to see its lowest levels since the pandemic.
Foot Locker teams with Stylitics as retailer taps AI technology to launch app-based closet builder solution
Foot Locker has developed, in partnership with Stylitics, a new AI powered closet builder, Fits, within its mobile app. In a LinkedIn post,
Michael Cera, Interim Head of Product Management and Design at Foot Locker, said: “AI is everywhere. But, at Foot Locker, we challenged ourselves to think about how to improve and make positive change to our customers shopping experience through the use of AI.”
He added: “We engaged with customers, really listened, and in partnership with Stylitics, developed a key new closet builder within the Foot Locker app - let me introduce you to Fits! Start with something you own. Discover personalised outfits built around it. See those looks come to life on a virtual model.”
Customers can upload or take a photo of something they own, discover complete outfits built around it, and visualise those looks on a virtual model. Paired with a cart addition from the model view, the aim is to make purchasing a whole outfit styled around your own products that much easier.
Cera concluded: “This was a collaborative effort across Experience Design, Product Management, E-comm, Brand, and Stylitics, and came to life exactly as we all set out to do. Download or open your Foot Locker app today and give it a try!”
Ikea stumps up £31.5 million as it looks to make UK fulfilment more efficient and reduce packaging waste
Ikea UK is investing £31.5 million across its Peterborough and Doncaster customer distribution centres (CDC) as the retailer aims to make online fulfilment more efficient and sustainable.
In Peterborough, new technology is packaging customer orders to size and reducing material usage by up to 30%, by preventing waste from oversized boxes and filling paper. In Doncaster, Ikea is trialling a new regional fulfilment capability, serving customers in the north and Scotland from a closer location to them.
The investments will strengthen Ikea’s UK fulfilment network as online sales account for 43.3% of total UK sales in financial year 2026. It is investing £30 million in new technology for its Peterborough CDC, with the upgrades taking place over a two-year period. As part of this, it has launched new PackSize technology to prevent waste from oversized cardboard boxes and filling materials by packaging customer orders to size. On average, the technology reduces material usage by up to 30% and void fill by up to 60%.
The technology is expected to increase the share of parcels processed through automation at the Peterborough CDC from 47% today to 75% in 2027, helping the fulfilment team prepare orders for delivery more efficiently. These additional orders would otherwise have been packaged by manually creating a packing carton which includes having to measure the article then creating the cartons to fit the order. Three drones and nests were introduced at the site in January to support inventory management. They scan each aisle in short cycles, helping Ikea to keep stock in the right place and meet customer demand.
Ikea is investing £1.5 million in trialling a new fulfilment capability at its Doncaster CDC. The site now fulfils orders for customers in the Gateshead, Edinburgh and Glasgow areas, with plans for Sheffield to follow. By fulfilling these orders from Doncaster rather than Peterborough, Ikea expects to reduce emissions from delivery journeys by an estimated 280 tonnes of CO2 annually. The new capability has created an additional 80 jobs at the Doncaster site.
US retailer Five Below taps poq platform for launch of new native iOS and Android mobile apps
poq has announced the launch of new native iOS and Android mobile apps for Five Below. Tiffany D’Amato, Vice President of Digital, Five Below, comments: “Our customers live on their phones, and these apps give them a faster, more engaging way to experience everything they love about Five Below.”
“Partnering with poq allowed us to bring that vision to life quickly and effectively, with a truly native experience built for our shoppers. We’re confident these apps will drive stronger customer engagement and long-term growth for the brand.”
Helen Slaven, Chief Revenue Officer at poq, says: “Five Below is exactly the kind of brand app commerce was made for, with a huge, engaged customer base and a shopping experience built on discovery. We are thrilled to partner with them to turn mobile into an owned channel that retains customers, grows lifetime value and scales with the business.”
A built-in price scanner lets shoppers scan an item in store and check its price and details on the spot, while personalised search helps customers explore the various products Five Below has to offer. Store aware features surface the nearest store and stock availability and push notifications, keep customers close to new arrivals and seasonal drops. The apps are built on poq’s platform and integrated with the Five Below commercetools commerce stack.
Firstwork secures $15 million Series A as startup looks to scale applied AI for frontline workforce ops
Firstwork, an AI platform for frontline workforce operations, has announced a $15 million Series A led by Earlybird Venture Capital, with participation from Legion VC, Deel Ventures and existing investors Gradient and Y Combinator. The round brings its total funding to date to $20 million.
Firstwork was founded in 2024 by Vardhan Kapoor and Shubham Choudhary. Kapoor previously led APAC at Remitly and strategy at Deliveroo Singapore, while Choudhary was a Director of Engineering at Deel after helping build Rippling’s global employment infrastructure.
More than 150,000 frontline workers now start work through Firstwork each month. Customers including Deel, Job&Talent, Relay, Wonolo and BGSF have cut the time workers and HR teams spend on each new hire by up to 90%, according to the company.
“The systems employers rely on were built to record what happened, not to actually do the work,” says Kapoor. “That leaves HR and operations teams spending enormous amounts of time chasing documents, coordinating across systems and supporting workers through processes that extend well beyond day one. Applied AI changes what is possible."
"We can now give every frontline worker the kind of support that used to be reserved for the top of the labour market, from the moment they apply through every stage of their employment.”

items.title: As a young man, magazines were my window to the world. That wonder will be lost when all the shops have gone | John Harris
items.summary: The closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. items.body:
Towards the end of the 1970s, the brief but spectacular career of those punk rockers and folk devils the Sex Pistols was followed by The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle, a rather tawdry drama-documentary. It recast their rise and fall as a huge scam, summed up by a slogan on a T-shirt worn by their former manager Malcolm McLaren: “Cash from Chaos”.
Back then, that motto was a neat representation of his personal brand of cultural mischief. But the culture always takes unexpected twists and turns – and 50 years on, an almost-identical maxim seems to be defining the fate of an increasing chunk of the British retail economy. While Andy Burnham pledges to restore life to town centres, a private equity outfit is busy buying up national retail chains and then shutting down scores of their outlets, while seemingly operating in line with its boss’s most celebrated quotation: “Where there’s chaos, there’s opportunity.”
Those words came from Jamie Constable, the owner of a set of businesses that includes Modella Capital, which specialises in “distressed investing” and “aggressive restructuring”. In 2024, Modella bought the craft supplies chain Hobbycraft – insisting on its “real commitment to bricks-and-mortar retail”, but then shutting 18 shops and triggering 600 job losses, while leaving redundancy costs to the taxpayer. Months later, it acquired the discount outlets branded as The Original Factory Shop, only for the entire chain to collapse. But its most ambitious move was its recent purchase of the 480 high-street shops that previously traded as WH Smith, rebranded by Modella as TG Jones (a completely made-up name, which it said would “keep that sense of a family business”), and the rapidly announced closure of up to 150 of them.
In September, 19 branches breathed their last, in such varied locations as Bath, Southend, Cardigan, Redhill and the Essex new town of Basildon. This month, the shutters are permanently falling in – among 23 places – Pinner, Truro, Inverness and Leek in Staffordshire. Thanks to their shortsighted folding into previous WH Smith premises, the closure plan will inevitably mean the loss of many local post offices: by early 2027, 70 will have gone. It will inevitably accelerate the decline of printed newspapers. But for me and many others, the key tragedy in this story is all about magazines, those gloriously tactile creations that played a crucial role in making many of us who we are.
I say that as someone who fell in love with this form of publishing as a child, via a weekly educational magazine called Look and Learn – stuffed, as I recall, with comic-strip versions of Dickens stories, and stuff about space exploration. By my early teens, I was an avid reader of Sounds, the Melody Maker and NME, the so-called weekly music papers that were really magazines whose ink came off on your fingers. Much to my amazement, between my 19th and 26th birthdays, I ended up successively working for all three – until, in 1995, I joined the now defunct company Emap Metro, which set enormous store by its mastery of glossy fortnightlies and monthlies.
Some of these names may mean precious little to younger readers, but spark a Proustian rush among older ones: Q, Smash Hits, Select (which I edited for three years), Sky, the metal and hard rock title Kerrang!, Big, Neon, FHM. Most have now closed, but three of the old stable are still standing, under different ownership: Kerrang!, which mostly lives online; the film bible Empire; and Mojo, the lovingly produced music magazine that I am thrilled to still write for.
Thirty years ago, we all knew that there was no better medium for in-depth interviews, or high-end photography. The management constantly asked us who our intended reader was, and what the future was likely to entail. Even the smallest cover-lines were pored over, as if the mere mention of Placebo or DJ Shadow might attract scores of newbies. And though a lot of us didn’t listen, we were told to never, ever put our magazines in sealed plastic bags (which, in line with a longstanding convention, would contain “free gifts”), for fear of losing the kind of punter who liked to browse before they bought.
And therein lies the TG Jones tragedy. The business has rightly acquired an utterly grim reputation, but is – or was – one reliable place to still find shelves full of printed content worthy of endless curiosity. And now? The culturally omnivorous twentysomething in Rickmansworth will no longer chance upon the latest edition of the cutting-edge music monthly the Wire, and thereby be inducted into a world of esoteric electronica and contemporary avant-garde jazz. The student-age customer in Ormskirk tiring of production-line pop may know nothing of the more substantial music covered by Mojo’s excellent competitor Uncut.
Would-be radicals will be unable to browse the printed iteration of Tribune; film freaks may be completely unaware of the in-depth, art-house wonders of Sight and Sound. Publishers will fall over themselves to alert us to subscription offers, but for a lot of people, they will be prohibitively expensive.
As George Orwell once put it, the UK is “a nation of stamp-collectors, pigeon-fanciers, amateur carpenters, coupon-snippers, darts-players, crossword-puzzle fans”. Products that reflect that enduring aspect of our national character are still at the core of magazine publishing, and why some titles still sell enviably: at the last count, for example, BBC Gardeners’ World sold a monthly average of 164,807 copies, while Country Living shifted 107,596. The broad women’s and fashion sector is also still here. It isn’t all over, by any means.
Still, one can easily imagine a Mark Zuckerberg-esque voice scoffing at all this as so much stone-age nonsense, and claiming that what printed magazines deliver can easily be either replicated or superseded on the internet. Experience often suggests otherwise: witness the fate of the once-independent online music magazine Pitchfork, bought out by the corporate publisher Condé Nast in 2015 and bizarrely folded into the workings of the men’s title GQ nine years later: a classic case of what we now know as enshittification. But there is an even bigger point here about how we now engage with the things we like and love, summarised in a forthcoming book titled Circulation: How Culture Moves in the Age of Algorithm by the Nashville-based US music insider David Macias, with a foreword written by Dan Clancy, the CEO of the livestreaming platform Twitch.
His argument is about music, but its logic applies across the cultural, recreational and sporting board. “The algorithm is great at finding me new music in the limited style I listen to,” he writes. “But it is really bad at showing me something new and different. My listening has become homogeneous, even though I can pick any album ever created.” This is the tedious prospect that the demise of the magazine will only accelerate – so after the high-street chaos has died down, we could be faced with an awful silence, broken only by the leakage from headphones playing the same things over and over again. And to speak the language of the insatiable capitalist, where will anyone find money in that?
- John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
items.body:
“Being able to take six weeks’ paid paternity leave, flexibly, made a huge difference to me and my family, giving me the time to support my partner and settle into being a new parent,” said Marks & Spencer employee Joe Erskine.
The food and clothing retailer increased its paternity leave offering from two to six weeks at full pay in 2024, meaning Erskine benefited from the new policy when his second child was born 17 months ago.
M&S and Tesco are among the retailers leading the way in offering enhanced paternity leave to their staff, new research has shown, highlighting the widening gap between the more family-friendly policies offered to new fathers working in the retail sector compared with those in construction, manufacturing and agriculture.
Both companies offer six weeks at full pay to employees, far outstripping the statutory two-week minimum paternity leave offer and making them among the most generous of UK blue-chip companies listed on the FTSE 100, according to figures compiled by campaign group The Dad Shift and Ian Dinwiddy of Inspiring Dads.
Privately owned companies Ikea, Lego and Virgin Media O2 now also offer more weeks of fully paid leave to new fathers.
The enhanced paternity leave offered by retailers including Asda, Waitrose and Lidl in recent years means that just five employers are responsible for upgrading parental leave for nearly 650,000 workers.
Retail businesses and the shop workers’ union Usdaw held a roundtable discussion in parliament, hosted by Labour MP Connor Rand, to discuss the transformation in working parents’ lives brought in by changes to parental leave.
Rand, who was a researcher for Usdaw prior to his election to parliament in 2024, said the entitlement was crucial for his family: “Through the ups and downs, I could bond with my son and support my partner because of paternity leave. Too many dads in our country can’t do this. That’s bad for them, bad for their partner and bad for their children. It must change.”
Campaigners have long argued that the UK has one of the least generous paternity leave offers in the world, ranked 40th out of 43 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries. Over two decades after paternity leave rights were introduced in Britain, they argue the country has fallen behind and now has the least generous entitlement in Europe.
Employed fathers in the UK are entitled to two weeks’ statutory paternity leave paid at £194.32 a week, or 90% of their average weekly earnings, whichever amount is lower, totalling less than half the national living wage.
Many companies offer enhanced paternity leave by topping up the statutory offer to full salary, in some cases for a longer period of time.
However, there is a growing disparity between different sectors of the economy. Analysis by The Dad Shift found that the construction sector employs around one in 10 working men, but only accounts for about one in 15 recipients of statutory paternity pay.
This could partly be because some construction workers are self-employed and currently have no entitlement to paid paternity leave, as is also the case for many of Britain’s agricultural workers, the majority of whom are self-employed.
Construction company JCB only offers two weeks’ full pay in paternity leave, although this has been increased from the three days it previously offered.
Engineering firm Rolls-Royce, which makes jet engines for planes, turbines for ships and small nuclear power plants, has a workforce that is more than 80% male but currently only offers two weeks’ fully paid leave.
More than 100 Labour MPs have called on Andy Burnham in recent weeks to commit to improving the UK’s paternity leave in the upcoming budget, warning that lowest-paid fathers are the hardest hit by inadequate paternity leave provision.
They are calling for the introduction of six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers. An 18-month government review of the UK’s parental leave system is expected to report later this year.
